speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS
subtopic: INCREASED EXPORTS OF LEAD AND ZINC-STUDY OF SMELTER CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I wish to announce that the government has approved the export from Pine Point in the Northwest Territories of additional quantities of high grade lead-zinc ore and zinc concentrates during the next two and three year periods. The application by Pine Point Mines Limited reflects a firm market position in these metals over this time period. We have approved the export of 90,000 tons per year of zinc metal contained in concentrates for a period of three years and 60,000 tons per year of high grade direct shipping ore.
These shipments will go to smelters in the United States. In addition, an earlier authority by which the government approved the export of 50,000 tons per year of elemental lead in concentrates to Japan for a period of ten years has been modified to allow the diversion of up to 15,000 tons of this amount to other markets during the next four years.
The result of these permits will be a very large increase in lead and zinc production in the immediate future. Not only will this produce very appreciable foreign exchange for Canada; it will also increase the volume of ore and concentrates moved by the Great Slave Lake Railway to more than double that anticipated before the mine went into production. It will be recalled that the government of Canada advanced the capital to build this railway. It is most encouraging to see this facility utilized to this extent.
When consideration was given to the applications for export, equal attention was given to the feasibility of increasing smelting facilities within Canada and particularly in the Northwest Territories. It is government policy to encourage processing of raw materials in Canada. On the basis of available information the case for establishing a smelter at Pine Point cannot be determined with certainty. There does seem to be a reasonable possibility that given adequate reserves and a continuation of present firm markets, such a
project might be realistic. The government is therefore engaging experienced consultants to undertake studies to determine the feasibility of the immediate construction of a smelter at Pine Point.
I am pleased to report that the mining company, Pine Point Mines Limited, and its parent organization, Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited, have given unqualified support to this approach and have agreed to co-operate by making available to the government's independent consultants, on a confidential basis, all information useful in such a study. Pyramid Mining Company Limited, which has recently announced development of lead-zinc ore reserves in the same region, and several other companies now exploring the area have also indicated their willingness to co-operate in the same way.
I shall not predict that a smelter can or will be built in the Pine Point area, but because of the tremendous significance such a development could have for the region, I wish to assure the house that the government intends to continue a very active role in this matter.
To carry out the study of the economic feasibility of a smelter at Pine Point, the government has decided to retain the internationally known firm of Canadian Bechtel Limited.

am sure all hon. members will be pleased with the minister's announcement to the effect that there is to be a considerable increase in the export of ores and concentrates from Pine Point in the Northwest Territories.
This, as the minister has said, will help to increase Canada's foreign exchange and we shall benefit to some extent as a result. However, I think the minister recognizes-and I hope the government recognizes-that the exporting of raw material is not going to make this country rich in the long run. In the extraction industries the amount of employment per unit of invested capital is relatively low. No country ever became rich by exporting its natural resources in their raw state. Employment and wealth come in the long run from the secondary and tertiary stages of development and manufacture.
I am sure the minister is to be congratulated when he says the government is looking into the feasibility of a smelter at Pine Point. I am glad to know that studies are to be made to determine the economic feasibility of this project. However, I would urge that the government give some thought to who will direct and operate the smelter. It seems to me this is an excellent opportunity for the Canada Development Corporation to undertake this project or to undertake it in partnership with a company which has the technical know-how.

Here Canada has an excellent opportunity to develop resources which belong to the crown in such a way that the Canadian people will reap the benefit not only from extracting the raw materials but from processing them here in Canada. I think it would be a great pity if the entire process of extraction and processing were turned over to private companies, particularly if they were private companies located outside Canada. We are, I repeat, very pleased with this development concerning our natural resources, but we would like them to be processed here first.

It is not possible to comment on the announcement in any detail as I did not receive notice of it. I have just checked with my office, and I believe I did not have prior notice, as did the others.

I am speaking of the vast area adjacent to Pine Point which we know as Wood Buffalo national park, an area which has been designated as a national park but which has nothing to do with park purposes. We would hope the minister would also release this area for the development of its natural resources, some of which are very vital and important to our economy.

maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must object to the approval of this report which asks that the committee be allowed to sit while the house is in session. If I were to ask its chairman why he wants this permission, he would tell me it was just in case it was needed. This is something to which we always objected. I recall that when we were in the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) objected to the move, as did the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) and as I did myself. But we were always defeated.
I know also that several Conservative members who requested it then, admit today that they should not have done so.
I feel that the motion recommending that the committee be allowed to meet while the

house is sitting should not have been presented and I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that it is not necessary. If the committee ever feels that it has to meet, it can always come back before the house and ask for leave to do so. We would examine the situation and find out the reason why the committee wants to meet. At present, nobody knows why. Some want to create a tradition which does not exist, and the proof that it does not exist is that we have the right to object when the motion is submitted.
That is why I object to the motion and ask the members of the house to go on record in this connection.
I think it is illogical that we should be obliged to miss the sittings of the house. We have work to do while the committee meets and if we grant the same privilege to all committees, then 22 committees will want to meet while the house is in session and there will be no members left to attend to the business of the house.
That is illogical and should not be allowed. I ask hon. members to reject this motion.

We will hear complaints about members not being in attendance here, and the answer to those complaints will be that they are in attendance at committee meetings but that fact will not be obvious to observers and the general public.
I should also like to support the stand that was taken some years ago by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). I did not understand the force of their arguments then but one can always learn, and I recognize now that they were very wise in the opposition they raised at that time. EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this has been an excellent debate so far although we are still waiting to hear from the government on some of the important issues that have been raised. I do not know whether I can take the debate to the same degree of rhetorical exuberance that it reached yesterday, but I do want to comment on an extraordinary statement made by the hon. member for York East. He said there were many serious problems in connection with the administration of justice in Canada and went on to say, as
Supply-Justice
found on page 1730 of Hansard of February
24:
I was not surprised to find some reaction to the proposal to split the department into two. I admire this move. I think this is reform because at least it is a change.
I know of nothing which indicates more the attitude of the government toward reform, namely, that all it needs to do is split departments into two.
During the course of the question period just ended I heard some comment about the government's stumbling and I think that is a pretty fair description. But even more than that, when the government has to face a problem it seems that its usual reaction is to fly into a fury of uncontrolled inaction and do nothing, something like a yo-yo, up and down, up and down but always in the same spot, never moving and never achieving any result.
I also heard the comments of the Minister of Justice concerning some of the serious questions raised respecting bankruptcy. The suggestion was made that this was a matter which could well be left to the provinces. I realize that so far as the Criminal Code is concerned-any member of the bar who has practised before the criminal courts will bear me out on this-by constitutional practice and by custom there is left to the provincial administrations acting through the various Attorneys General the prosecution of criminal cases, especially those arising under the Criminal Code. It is also a known fact, however, that with regard to matters coming under other federal statutes, for example, the Excise Act, the Narcotic Act and the Immigration Act, the almost invariable practice is for the Minister of Justice to appoint counsel who prepares these cases and prosecutes where necessary.
An examination of the Bankruptcy Act indicates that a large number of matters are referred to which constitute offences under that act, and the practice has been followed that such matters be referred to appropriate counsel. Those of us who were here in the last parliament know there are counsel appointed by the Minister of Justice. We all had a chance to examine a very interesting list which was prepared by another minister of the Crown who has since gone on to a higher position and we know that the list included the names of those who were agents of the Minister of Justice. Therefore I assume there are competent counsel in this country, and if there are offences under this act I suggest it is through the medium of the minister and

February 25, 1968
Supply-Justice
his officials that these prosecutions should take place.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the utmost use will be made of the standing committee which has been set up. I am not referring to the select committee which the Solicitor General mentioned but the standing committee which will be dealing with various matters concerning the administration of justice, no matter under whose department they may fall.
There has been reluctance on the part of the Prime Minister to refer the matter of Mr. Spencer to a royal commission. I shall deal with that later. But even though I am not a member of the standing committee, although I hope to exercise my rights to appear before it from time to time and conduct certain examinations, I trust that the committee, if it sees its duty as I see it, will call Mr. Spencer before it, as it has every right to do, when it is examining the estimates of the department for the fiscal year 1966-67. I see no barrier to the committee calling Mr. Spencer before it and conducting a thorough and careful examination of all the facts about which hon. members, particularly members of the opposition, have shown such great concern.
If no other medium is established, I also hope the committee will call before it the superintendent of bankruptcy and such other officials as it sees fit. This is not a matter that needs to be referred to the committee by the house. As I understand the rules and practice under which these committees are constituted, there will be a mandatory reference of the estimates to the committee and during the process of examination of those estimates there are sure to be items under which it will be possible to call these people for that close and detailed examination which is so essential in order that the people of the country can be reassured, if it is possible to reassure them, about these serious matters that have come to light.
I now wish to talk about the Combines Investigation Act, which was discussed yesterday. I understand this is a matter which comes strictly within the purview of the President of the Privy Council.
During the time he was minister of justice I asked him one or two questions, both on estimates and orders of the day, which indicated that in my opinion, from an examination of the jurisprudence in this field, there was great doubt whether the constitutional practice of resting the operations of the Combines Investigation Act and the restrictive trade practices jurisdiction on the

Criminal Code was satisfactory. True enough. I know that decisions of the past have suggested this may have been proper at that time, but my recollection is that the minister intimated to me that he and his officials were giving serious consideration to deciding whether or not the jurisdiction could be broadened by invoking the provisions of the B.N.A. Act, section 91, under the head, "the regulation of trade and commerce".
I do not know to what extent this has progressed, but from an examination of the decided cases and having in mind the purpose for which this legislation was designed I believe that it has failed to achieve what we set out to obtain many years ago when the legislation was first introduced.
In this connection an interesting article appeared in the last edition of the Alberta Law Quarterly. It is by Professor MacDonald, assistant professor of the faculty of law at Queens University. At page 67 of the Quarterly he deals at length with the question of criminality and the Canadian anticombines law. I shall not go into detail. He makes some very prudent observations, and an examination of the article supports the view I take that if we are going to use this type of measure effectively we will have to proceed on a much wider basis.
I am not here to suggest how this might be done. It may be essential to have consultation with the provincial governments to see whether or not the constitution is in fact a rigid barrier to the type of jurisdiction we need. There may have to be consultation with the provinces to see if they will lend their efforts and we might have some kind of joint program. I am inclined to think-and I mention this with diffidence because I dealt with the subject some few days ago-that it may be possible now.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
I think it is a known fact that the Supreme Court is now the final arbiter in matters of constitutional practice in this country. As I understand the view expressed by some of the judges of the Supreme Court and the Privy Council, they are not necessarily bound by the decisions of the past. In other words, the principle of stare decisis is not a principle which should apply to constitutional matters. I should like to see the most careful review of the combines legislation to see whether it can be effective and to see whether there may be some measure of control without attaching the stigma of unreality in matters which involve decisions which have to be
February 25, 1966

made by large corporations and which can have a very serious and detrimental effect on the people of this country.
I think the way we should approach it is to consider whether or not we should broaden the jurisdiction by invoking the trade and commerce section of the B.N.A. Act. Some time or other I would ask the President of the Privy Council to give us his view and indicate the extent to which the investigation by his officials, which he indicated to me would take place has progressed.
I should like to deal very briefly with one other matter before I revert to the Spencer case. During the course of the report of the Auditor General reference was made on several occasions by this official to the fact that in his opinion there had been a number of breaches of the Judges Act by reason of the practice which has grown up of providing for judges who are appointed to various tribunals a measure of financial consideration which is designated as being a cost of living allowance. As the ministers know, it is quite definite that the Judges Act provides that there shall be no remuneration given to an occupant of the bench over and above his salary. The Auditor General's opinion-he has had access to counsel in Toronto and in Montreal-is buttressed by the report he has received from these people, as well as by the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee, to the effect that the payment of sums in the amount of say $100 a day contains an element of remuneration which is contrary and repugnant to the provisions of the Judges Act.
This may be a small issue, Mr. Chairman, but the government comes to the people in an effort to secure the greatest measure of law and order. It is for it to put its house in order in every way and certainly, sir, a suggestion which has been made on several occasions that judges occupying the positions they do have not been following the law because of this fact is, I think, something which should be considered by the department.
I should like to deal now with the Spencer case. I think it is a tremendous tribute to this parliament and to this country that this poor unfortunate individual, for whom I hold no brief, has had his case ventilated in the fullest detail or at least to some extent. As a result of a request made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the members of the opposition the Prime Minister made a statement with regard to Mr. Spencer. It is a statement I do not accept, but at least he was
Supply-Justice
compelled to make the statement. I already have suggested that in my opinion, inasmuch as the Prime Minister has indicated that noinquiry will be held, that we at least should have the benefit of Mr. Spencer's appearance before the standing committee. I see no reason that this should not be done and therefore I will reserve any further comments on the question of the rightness of the action taken in the hope, in which I hope I will be supported by members of the house, that he will be appearing before the committee.
I do want to say something with regard to what I think is a very serious by-product of this case. I have noted som6 of the interventions made during the course of this session in respect of the Spencer case. The first time it was brought up was on January 21 when the Leader of the Opposition asked the Minister of Justice to comment on it. At that time the minister made what I considered an extraordinary statement supporting and corroborating the position he had taken on a television broadcast, which might have been excused at that time under the circumstances that prevailed but which I hardly think could be excused when given calmly and deliberately in response to a question in the house. The minister said as found on page 85 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, there is no specific law or statute that covers the question of surveillance; it flows from the ordinary administration of the law by law enforcement officers.
Then the minister went on to deal further with this matter. I was prompted to ask the Prime Minister as a supplementary question whether he asserted on behalf of the government that a general right exists to scrutinize and keep under surveillance any citizen on the basis of what the government thinks that citizen may do in the future. This line of thought on the part of the government, which is clearly indicated and clearly delineated in those questions and answers was followed further by the Minister of Justice on January 31 as recorded on page 425 of Hansard where he made this statement;
As to surveillance, I said, in the course of a television program, that there would be surveillance on this man as long as he remains in Canada. It would be irresponsible not to keep such a man under surveillance fitted to the needs of the case. As already mentioned, security operations are primarily preventive in nature and success must often depend on surveillance.
Further comments were then made. Again, Mr. Chairman, on February 8 the Minister of Justice, in response to a question by the right

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: When was the first reference made to the fact that this was being done for his own protection?

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
The question has been asked when the suggestion was first raised that this surveillance was being carried out for the protection of the individual. So far as my research has indicated, the first reference was made by the Prime Minister in his statement to the house the other day.
I suggest there are enough encroachments on individual liberties today. Some of them are essential, some of them are covered by legislation such as the Customs Act, the Excise Act, the Immigration Act, and the War Measures Act if it is ever invoked. However, these are all matters in respect of which parliament has spoken.
I should like the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice before this debate is concluded to indicate to the house whether it is their view that the executive of this country, represented by the cabinet and their appointed officials, have the right to place any individual under the type of surveillance that is envisaged here without going through the due process of law under the authority of a statute which this parliament has made. It might well be that I might choose to make an inflammatory speech in this house. Does that mean that I could be followed or placed under continuous surveillance? Hon. gentlemen may say that such an idea is farfetched. I do not think it is because the principle is precisely the same. I hope that before this debate is concluded we will be given a clear and precise answer with regard to this serious situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can assure the house and the hon. gentleman who just rose in anticipation of being the next speaker that my remarks will be fairly brief. Not being a member of the legal profession I normally prefer, during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Justice, to sit and listen to the members of the house who because of their vocations are necessarily much more familiar with the Department of Justice, the administration of justice and all the other legal involvements that are confusing to the average backbencher.
That does not mean, Mr. Chairman, that I have been unable to appreciate the debate thus far. I share the view of the hon. member who has just taken his seat that in general the calibre of speeches made since our consideration of the estimates of the Department
February 25, 1966

of Justice began has been on a fairly high plane. I suppose they have been of interest to me because each and every speaker has added to my limited store of knowledge about the Department of Justice and the administration of justice in Canada. I must admit at the outset that I have a very limited knowledge of what is basically federal and what is basically provincial jurisdiction.
I was particularly impressed by the contribution of the hon. member for Kamloops, in fact, to the extent that I re-read his speech this morning. Not only did it reflect a thorough knowledge of the Department of Justice, not only did it contain what I thought were very objective criticisms of the department, but it could be considered as a lesson to the average member who wants to make an effective and objective contribution to the debate. I say this because there was a lot of meat in the speech made by that hon. member and because it was delivered without the belligerence that unfortunately a lot of us think is necessary to make a speech effective.
I cannot help but contrast the depth of the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops with the speech I was privileged to hear a little earlier delivered by the hon. member for Bow River, my old sparring partner of last session. I should like to refer to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops a little later in my speech if time permits.
I should like particularly to make reference to one paragraph which I think is valid in that it points out the dangers that may result from the exercise of legal authority within the Department of Justice. I intend to read that paragraph from Hansard because I think in it the hon. member for Kamloops implies very strongly that some of the problems that faced the former minister of justice leading to the Dorion inquiry could easily have been avoided had there been a form of mechanism within the department for the exchange of information, perhaps through joint meetings of the officers of the various branches that make up the ministry of justice.
This paragraph is very important so far as I am concerned because it explains to me why no action was taken against Hal Banks between the years 1958 and 1962. I do not suggest this in a sarcastic manner but rather objectively because although I am not a lawyer I realize there is a very sharp line of distinction between what is immoral and what is considered under the law to be illegal.
Supply-Justice
The hon. member for Peace River made a very excellent speech a few minutes ago regarding what is commonly referred to as the Spencer case. It contained much food for thought and emphasized what I have sought to emphasize when speaking in this House of Commons on occasion, the rights of individuals no matter how humble they may be. If a man like Spencer cannot have his case presented in the House of Commons, the highest court of the land, where can he turn for protection? If this high court becomes so callous that we are not interested in the rights of the individual it is time for us to sit back and take stock. The individual to whom I refer could be a Spencer or a Banks, and I am sure that the lawyers of this house, who are not as emotionally involved in personalities because of their background and training, can understand this point better than I.
Before I lose the trend of my thought I should like to make the original point I intended to make in this debate, and I draw it to the attention of the minister. I have had more than one constituent come to me with complaints of a similar nature, not because I am a lawyer but because I am a member of parliament like every other member of the house. I should like to give one example. Approximately three weeks ago a young man of 34 years of age, married and with three children, a man devoted to recreational activities in the community, active in one of our social welfare organizations, a man who has worked extremely hard for the company which employs him, suddenly realized that his hard work was to be recognized and that he was to be promoted from an average position to one of trust within his company.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
He had worked for this company for 12 years and had an impeccable record. However, he found to his amazement that because of his new position of trust the company had gone back into his record-they felt this to be necessary despite his 12 years of service-and after a thorough investigation of this young man's past had discovered that at the age of 19 he had been arrested and convicted of a common assault which occurred outside a Montreal nightclub. At that time the young man served a few days in prison. That blot is still on his record 15 years after the offence. His crime against society is no greater than that.
Being a belligerent Irishman, Mr. Chairman, I can recall half a dozen occasions when but for the grace of God my name would also

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
have been in the permanent files of the K.C.M.P. This man has not only been refused promotion but it has been suggested that in the opinion of the pompous board of directors he should find another position in the next 60 days. This is not an isolated case; this sort of situation has been brought to my attention on half a dozen occasions. This is not the case of a man who has broken the law two, three, four or five times thereby establishing a pattern or a tendency to become a criminal. It is the case of a man who has broken the law once and that once when he was a teen-ager.
When one inquires around parliament one is told that there may be a way in which his record can be cleansed. But is there a way? If there is a way, why do we have to be furtive about it? Why do we not amend the laws of the land to make some provision to cleanse the record of a young man or girl who after an offence has served society well for five or ten years and has not shown any tendency to repeat an act of violence or break the laws of the land? In those circumstances why cannot their criminal record be wiped out as is done in the case of juveniles? I am not a lawyer, Mr. Chairman, and cannot even offer a suggestion because I feel very inadequate at the moment.
I should like to refer to another case which came to my attention last Friday. This case affects me deeply. I arrived home as usual at 20 minutes to eight and as usual the telephone rang at 15 minutes to eight. A distraught mother had called to inform me that her young son had been arrested two hours earlier and she could not get sufficient information with regard to what would happen to her boy. So I went to the local police station and found that her son together with four other boys of my community had been detained or arrested, whichever is the correct word, for breaking into the local high school.
After breaking into the high school they had thrown school books around, stolen 92 cents and finally, very unfortunately, had set fire to a wing of the school. The fire resulted in considerable material damage. Certainly they should have been picked up and detained or arrested. But what concerns me more, and I have no answer for this problem, is that I found on investigating the matter with the police that this young man 15 years of age, who as far as I understand comes from a normal home and is one of three or four children, was first arrested or detained-I do not know the right word when talking about juveniles-in the community of Verdun

at the age of 10 and was re-arrested at the age of 12 and again at the age of 14. At the time of this last offence he was 15.
Considered by themselves each of these charges was perhaps not too serious but I feel they denote a pattern of behaviour if this is the word to use. To a father of a boy of 12 who has just discovered "Treasure Island" or "Huckleberry Finn" it seems inconceivable that a youngster of 10 or 12 years of age can run afoul of the law. But it happens. What disturbs me more as a father is the fact that, this tendency to rebel against society having been discovered in this young man at the age of 10 or 12, nothing had been done about it. It is all very well to say it is the parents' fault, and perhaps it is. But it is also our fault because if young children of 10 or 12 commit this type of offence there should be some medium at our disposal whereby they can be helped. The medium may be either provincial or federal but something should be done to prevent this type of conduct in the future on the part of a young person and find out what is troubling him.
The thought went through my mind as I sat in that cold, dirty police station discussing this question that, if something is not done for this boy who is only 15 years of age, by the time he is 17, 19 or 21 he may be arrested on a charge of murder committed while holding up a drug store. It was at that moment I came to the conclusion that when we vote in this house on the question of capital punishment I shall vote for the abolition of the death sentence. I shall do this because somewhere along the line we have failed that young person of 10 or 12 years of age. Not only did his parents fail him but so did society.
I am not criticizing the social welfare courts of Quebec. I have a great deal to do with them as a private citizen looking after my constituents, more particularly as an aider-man than as a member of the house. I have been filled with admiration for two judges whom I have no hesitation naming, Judge Long and Judge Nicholson. The last time I saw them they were working in cramped quarters; they were overworked, overburdened, overtaxed. They bear a heavy burden day in and day out because of problems such as this.
I say to the members of the legal profession in this house that there is something wrong when this sort of situation exists. There has to be a better way of dealing with a juvenile of 10, 12 or 13. Perhaps I have no
February 25, 1966

right to raise this question or challenge the authorities to find an answer because I do not have any answer. I do not even know where to start. My contact with this segment of society is limited, unlike the contact of members of the legal profession.
I leave this matter with the ministers responsible as food for thought. It is time we developed a more acute conscience and stopped paying lip service to the problem by saying, "Let the schoolteachers rectify the situation" or "What do you expect? This boy comes from a broken home." The answer is not in building more penitentiaries, making them bigger, more spacious and mollycoddling a person aged 25 or 30 who is sent to penitentiary. The problem begins when a little boy of 10 is picked up for stealing a package of gum or because he showed his resentment of school by breaking into it, not breaking out of it.
I come back to the words of the hon. member for Kamloops who pointed out, 1 think quite reasonably and accurately, that whether we have one Minister of Justice or the jurisdiction is split into two or three fields the government and the ministers concerned must make certain that one hand knows what the other is doing. The hon. member stressed the point that the advisers of the department must know what the R.C.M.P. reports are all about. I will not read the passage at length. Hon. members can find the words at page 1725 of Hansard. I believe I have properly paraphrased the words used by the hon. member or he would have corrected me.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
This brings me back to the Banks affair, to which the hon. member for Bow River likes to refer when he is running out of material of a more serious nature. As reported at page 11406 of Hansard for last year the then hon. member for Carleton, Mr. Francis, asked a series of questions about Hal Banks. There were eight questions in all. These eight questions established the fact that the insidious problem of the bully, Hal Banks, was apparent to the Department of Justice as early as 1958.

The point I tried to make earlier was that there is a distinction between having suspicions against a man and charging a man. The department must feel certain they can convict him, even though everyone in Canada knows that the man is morally irresponsible and morally guilty, before they charge him. I imagine there would be a distinction in the mind of the layman between being morally guilty and being suspected guilty, if my English explains my thought properly.
From listening to the hon. member for Kamloops yesterday I would say, though I am only guessing, that when he discussed the R.C.M.P. reports on Hal Banks between 1958 and 1962 he did so, as he said yesterday-I am not contradicting his words-with the senior officers of his department and came to the conclusion that no matter how advisable and wonderful it would be to bring Mr. Banks to justice and to prosecute him on the evidence then available, nevertheless in his opinion and in the opinion of the law officers of the land there was not sufficient evidence to do so.
I applaud the then Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Kamloops, for not bowing to public opinion and bringing Hal Banks before the courts of the land when in his opinion and in view of the advice which he sought and received there was not sufficient evidence to convict this man. That requires courage.

speechtext:
As usual the hon. member for Bow River has to have the last word and

February 25, 1965

I concede it to him. We are all friends here. If he wants me to criticize the speech he made yesterday I can do so effectively but it was not an important enough speech for me to devote my time to it. I am more interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops.
What I am trying to say is that it takes courage not to bow to political expediency. If it took four years for the Conservative government to set up a royal commission to investigate the affairs of Hal Banks, knowing the reputation of the then minister of justice I am sure there would have been no hesitation on his part in 1958, 1959, 1960 or 1961 to bring Hal Banks to justice if in his opinion there had been sufficient evidence upon which to do so. I am sure he felt in his own mind that morally the man was guilty of something but that to prove it was another matter. Therefore I commend his restraint in those days.
I think that is borne out by anyone who refers to the answers to the questions posed by the then member for Carleton. I do not want to take too much time on this matter but the first question he asked, as reported at page 11406 of Hansard for February 17, 1965, was:
Did the Department of Justice, in 1958, through the R.C.M.P., conduct an investigation to determine if Hal Banks had been employing intimidation and violence in the furtherance of union activities?
The answer was:
Yes. In November, 1958, the Minister of Justice instructed the R.C.M.F. to conduct an exploratory investigation-[DOT]
and so on and so forth.
The second question was:
Did the government on February 23, 1959, as a result of the aforementioned investigation, receive a full account of the conspiracy which resulted in the Walsh beatings?
The answer was:
The R.C.M.P. advise that on February 23, 1959, they forwarded a preliminary report to the Minister of Justice, under secret cover, outlining the findings of their investigation into the activities of Hal Banks, which included an account of the conspiracy to beat Captain Walsh.
The third question was:
Was any action taken by the government of that day to bring Banks to trial as a result of that evidence?
The simple answer was "No".
I come to another question:
Was another report, which included a further account of the Walsh conspiracy, sent on June 14, 1961, to the government by the Department of Justice?

The answer was:
The R.C.M.P. advise that on June 14, 1961, they forwarded a further report to the Minister of Justice, under secret cover, which enlarged on their findings with respect to Hal Banks and the general picture of the S.I.U. activities, including further information with respect to the beating of Captain Walsh.
The rest of the questions go on to lead up to the establishement of the royal commission which investigated the disruption and problems of the waterfront. I find no fault with the fact that it took three or four years to establish the commission or that the minister of justice of that day did not feel the time for action was appropriate. But the hon. member for Bow River has constantly harped on Hal Banks and his relationship with the Liberal party, intimating to those who do not know differently that the Liberal government in. some way conspired to keep Hal Banks in Canada.
The hon. member for Bow River will get up and say: "That is not my point at all. My point is, how did he get bail and then get out of the country?"
I say to the hon. member for Bow River that Hal Banks, regardless of who he was and regardless of his record, as an individual was entitled to the full protection of the law, as is Mr. Spencer with regard to whom the hon. member for Bow River made an eloquent and moving address two days ago. According to' the judge who presided at the trial, Hal Banks was entitled to bail. I have only to quote once more the words of the hon. member for Bow River, words with which l agree-I agree with him more often than I disagree-in which he emphasized the importance of maintaining the independence of the judicial system in Canada. Yet he averred yesterday that the judge, through some devious means used by our party-the hon. member kept referring to shoving things under the rug-conspired to give this man not only bail but to see that after he got bail he left the country. However, the fact remains that Mr. Banks was entitled to bail. The judge was also entitled to set bail. Hal Banks was entitled to the same rights that Mr. Spencer should enjoy as an ordinary, common citizen of this country.
The hon. member referred yesterday to Dr. Marcoux and also to one of the ministers on the front bench. He might have gone all the way and said the present Minister of Transport. What are the facts? Hon. members want all the facts. They can read the speech made by the hon. member for Lapointe last night. The facts may be embarrassing not to this

party but to the hon. gentleman's party. I thought that this was all part of good old [DOT]electioneering and I was a little surprised when the hon. member brought the matter [DOT]up in the house of Commons.
The fact remains that Dr. Marcoux made very serious allegations which should have been investigated.

When Dr. Marcoux went up and down the province of Quebec making these statements Mr. Wagner called him to his office, provided him with police protection and demanded and obtained a full investigation into the allegations which had been made by Dr. Marcoux. Rivard was in jail. Now he is accusing the government for speeding up those proceedings. If I am a little confused it is not only because I might be a little stupid in not understanding this-

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: I must agree with you there.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River said that between the years 1958 and 1962 there were citizens of Canada who were afraid to exert their civil liberties and privileges and to testify in the courts of the land.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE

We all know why they were afraid. They were afraid of being beaten up. Is it not the function of the Department of
February 25, 1966

Justice to provide protection? By the hon. member's own words he admits that the Department of Justice did not provide protection between 1958 and 1962. People who were afraid then found the courage to appear before the commission after 1962 when we were in power. I am not going to insult anybody in this house by saying that since we have come to power everybody is free, because speaking as an individual I suggest that the Spencer case raises the question in my mind whether the rights of Canadian individuals are properly protected. Did not the hon. member for Bow River inquire whether the only reason that no action was taken against Hal Banks was that people were afraid to come forward and testify? I would also say this in answer to my hon. friend's question. I feel more inclined to thing, after listening last night to the hon. member for Kamloops, that the reason Hal Banks was not brought to trial between 1958 and 1962 was the opinion of the Minister of Justice at that time, based on the co-operation which he believes is now non-existent between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and senior officers of the department, that regardless of whether Mr. Banks was guilty there was not sufficient evidence available to warrant his being brought to trial.

speechtext:
If the hon. member from Kamloops does not rise I will. I do not intend to follow the hon. member for Verdun who said he was not a lawyer and was therefore, "all wet". He is not. The hon. member also said in a moment of embarrassing modesty that he was "a little stupid". He is obviously not that. I must say I admire the hard and losing struggle he waged trying to be nonpolitical.
I rise to deal fairly briefly with one matter, namely, the Spencer case. I rise because in my respectful submission the Prime Minister of this country made on Wednesday a statement which was not only astonishing but outrageous in its expression of disregard for basic principles of justice and civil liberty. I rise also because of a personal experience in connection with a client some years ago to which I wish to refer.
What the Prime Minister said in effect was that he had studied this case, looked into it, discussed it with his ministerial colleagues, given many hours to its consideration, and was therefore in a position to assure the house that Mr. Spencer was treated fairly. In fact, the Prime Minister says he was treated with scrupulous fairness.
What the Prime Minister is saying to the house and to the country is that when he, the Prime Minister, looks into a decision and decides it was a fair one that closes the matter. He arrogated to himself on Wednesday the attitude and the power of an unrivalled autocrat. He showed qualities of presumption and arrogance which make me sad as a Canadian, for no one person, no matter how high his estate in the country, has the right to say: I am the one, and when I tell you I have investigated a decision and it is just, you are to accept that it is just.
I have never in all my years of studying political science heard or read a statement so outrageous and so derisive of respect for civil
[The Deputy Chairman.]
liberties. In the area of civil liberties no one person can arrogate such powers to himself. I say, without apologizing for dragging it in, that one could be inclined to pay more attention to the assurances of the right hon. gentleman if one had not had experience of his bad judgment in previous affairs of this sort, experiences with the Liberal party in its behaviour toward the Japanese during the war and its behaviour in the Gouzenko investigation. If we had not had these experiences and the example disclosed yesterday of the unrivalled, unlimited and shabbiest use of pork barrel politics in appointments to the other place, we would be inclined to pay a little more attention to the statements of the right hon. gentleman.
Lest anyone misunderstand me let me say this: I assure the house that the other place is welcome to Mr. Hazen Argue, that discredited politician and anachronistic appendage of Parliament, as far as I am concerned. I would merely draw attention to the fact that we have made progress in our civilization. The thirty pieces of silver have now become half a million dollars, which is what Mr. Argue has been paid for being what he was.

I should like to put before the committee very briefly the considerations which led me to this conclusion-
To the conclusion that an inquiry is not necessary. Then he gave three reasons. I have never, Mr. Chairman, in appearances before judges, before boards-indeed my memory goes back to my high school days and undergraduate days in university-heard more obviously invalid reasons in support of any conclusion. His first reason is:
-Mr. Spencer himself has admitted, voluntarily admitted, Improper activities-
Who knows that? How does the Prime Minister know it? Was he there? Did he hear the voluntary admission? To whom was that voluntary admission made? By what reason does the Prime Minister think that the members of the committee should accept that statement? Is it merely because he makes it?
February 25, 1966

He makes the statement obviously without any personal knowledge whatever, accepting some note given to him no doubt by some underling of the Minister of Justice. A more outrageous suggestion as a reason for accepting his conclusion is hardly imaginable.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
