maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
An hon. member says it is not true. I have not the faintest notion whether or not it is true but I do know that no responsible leader of this country should make such a statement when he was not present at the time the conversation took place and offer that statement as an excuse for parliament to accept his conclusion. Having made one spurious suggestion he goes on to another:
In the second place it was Mr. Spencer himself who disclosed his identity-

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
My leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the other day punctured that unctuous inaccuracy, Mr. Chairman, and I choose my words carefully. Obviously the man was branded. He was fired. What more active part does the right hon. gentleman want to play in identifying Mr. Spencer? Does he want to make a trip to Vancouver and point him out to the R.C.M.P.? Is that the only way in which his government becomes involved? It is a gross misreading of the facts to make that statement. To cap it all, to cap this entire structure of disregard for the most elementary procedures of decent and civilized justice, the right hon. Prime Minister said:
-before a final decision was taken to dismiss Mr. Spencer he was given a hearing-
Just listen to the use of that word "hearing".
-by a senior official of the Civil Service Commission, at which he had every opportunity to state his case.
I challenge any hon. member, I challenge the Minister of Justice, I challenge the Solicitor General to give the committee another case of sheer, utter nonsense that compares with this statement in terms of any decent, legal inquiry. Some member of the Civil Service Commission met with Mr. Spencer, had some conversations with him and the right hon. gentleman calls that a hearing. What an outrageous use of words.
If the right hon. gentleman did not mean to mislead the committee, because he knew perfectly well hon. members could not be misled, in my respectful submission he could only have meant to mislead the people of Canada by using this kind of language to describe
Supply-Justice
that kind of conversation between an official and Mr. Spencer.
Finally, having given these completely invalid, unacceptable explanations for his conclusion, the right hon. gentleman then misrepresented the request that was made of him. May I interject to say that in all my political activity I have always taken the position in speeches outside this country that, whatever party I belong to, the Prime Minister of this country is the leader of this country. It therefore hurts me beyond words to find the leader of this country behaving in the shabby way that the Prime Minister has done in the case of Mr. Spencer. I say "shabby" because after giving us these spurious reasons for rejecting it he misrepresents the request that was made of him.
At the bottom of the right hand column on page 1682 the Prime Minister said:
If these procedures could not be used in this way in appropriate circumstances, or if all the details arising out of them must be made public, and names made public, then the protection of our national security against subversive action would be greatly prejudiced if not made impossible.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Right.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
This is right if it were true, but no one asked the right hon. gentleman for a public inquiry. The request of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and of the Leader of the Opposition was for an inquiry by a third party, if necessary in camera. No one requested that this inquiry be open to the public and the press. The request made of the government was for a hearing, as it were, before a third person, before a competent tribunal and in camera if necessary. No one is interested in hearing names as was suggested by the right hon. gentleman.
This brings me to an actual example I want to place before the committee. In my professional capacity as counsel for labour unions I happened to be involved in such a matter some years ago. I shall deliberately leave out names and make my references a little vague so that the person involved cannot be identified. An employee of one of the federal crown corporations in right of Canada was refused something to which he was entitled under the collective agreement on the express ground of security. We took the matter to arbitration under the collective agreement.
We could not get anywhere in arbitration because the lawyers for the crown corporation involved refused to give us any reasons.

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
They said, "Security reasons make it impossible for us to tell you why this person did not get what, under the collective agreement, he was entitled to."
With the assistance of the chairman of the board of arbitration we then saw the then minister of justice, the hon. member for Kamloops. He did, and I give him credit for doing so, precisely what we have not been able to persuade the government to do now. We persuaded him to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the facts of that case in camera.
The person appointed royal commissioner was the dean of law at the University of British Columbia. The accusers of my client-I will call him that-were not there when we were there nor were we there when they were there, but this entirely independent person who had no axe to grind, who could not be motivated by a desire to protect any underling who had gone wrong or to cover up anything else, who could be accepted as completely independent and disinterested, heard the other side and then, when I appeared with the employee, gave me information as to the facts he had received which in his view could be released to me.
He did not give me facts, if he had any-I do not know whether or not he had-which in his judgment it would not have been wise to give me from the point of view of Canada's security. However, my client felt he had a thoroughly good hearing because the commissioner gave him every chance to explain every question that was raised.
The result of that inquiry-I emphasize this and I ask the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General to note it-was that the person involved was cleared by the dean of law of the University of British Columbia and compensated for his loss.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
At that time the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and officers of the Department of Justice had reached the conclusion that the man was guilty. It was only this independent inquiry which removed that guilt. I ask, Mr. Chairman, what possible harm to the security of Canada could conceivably occur if the dean of the University of British Columbia or a member of the judiciary of Canada were given the information which the minister has, heard this information in camera, listened to Mr. Spencer and his counsel in camera, and then told the members of this house and people of Canada what his conclusions were. If that were done by a third, disinterested

person, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I am pretty sure, said on Wednesday, and we were told that Mr. Spencer was properly dismissed, then so far as we are concerned that would be the end of the matter.
I again appeal to the minister and the Solicitor General and through them to the right hon. Prime Minister to institute such an inquiry, because in civil liberties even more than anywhere else the appearance of justice and the fact of justice must coincide.
I should like to say, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the most unfair part of the treatment of Mr. Spencer, so far as I have been able to see, is the fact that he has been deprived of his pension. His age, I understand, is 57. He has been dismissed from his job and his pension is taken from him.
As the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam quite properly has said, the government is imposing a fine on this man without a trial. This should be looked into. In other words, I am suggesting there be an independent inquiry both in respect of whether or not this man is guilty, and second, in respect of whether or not even if he is, it is fair and just to deprive him of his pension. Dismissal is surely punishment enough and there is no need to add to that punishment by depriving him of what he has earned as he worked. I do not know the gentleman, but this action well may leave him in terrible penury.
I do not like to be sentimental about these things but I do remind hon. members, Mr. Chairman, if they need reminding-and I am sure they do not-that ever since the rights of individuals have been recognized by our society we have learned time and time again that the easiest thing in the world is to neglect those rights and to neglect them in unctuous self-righteousness. It is precisely those people who beat their breasts and say I have considered everything, I have looked at every angle, I have studied each word, I have gone into every detail and this is my conclusion-it is precisely those who make this kind of assertion who most easily ignore or innocently overlook the rights of people into whose lives they have so carefully looked.
We have also learned over the centuries that when civil liberties have been recognized in democratic countries the only way to make sure they are not eroded is to take a stand every time they are attacked. I submit that it is the high duty of the government and of the
February 25, 196S

Prime Minister to make sure that they do not leave even a possibility of suspicion that injustice and unfairness have ruled in the Spencer case. I appeal, despite the decision the Prime Minister has announced, that he and his ministerial colleagues reconsider and accept the suggestion that a third person be appointed to make an in camera inquiry into this whole case.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks about fraudulent bankruptcies in Canada and in the province of Quebec in particular.
In 1962, I asked the Minister of Justice to make an investigation in that regard, but he did not do anything. I asked the same thing again in 1963 without any results. Bankruptcies kept on happening. The situation has not improved in the province of Quebec. It is a terrible disaster, especially with regard to the province of Quebec.
It is a very good year for those experts in fraudulent bankruptcies. Mr. Chairman, we must put a stop to the exploitation carried on by those crooks in the business world. The Minister of Justice must do something, because the situation is serious.
Several murders have been committed in the last five or six years; people have disappeared from the surface of the earth without leaving any trace. Several were shot to death by notorious bandits. The Department of Justice has got to do something.
Reference was made to the Spencer case. In my opinion, the case of the fraudulent bankruptcies is ten times worse and yet the Department of Justice has still not done anything in this matter.
The fraudulent bankruptcy racket is so widespread, so complex in its organization and so fantastically far-reaching in our part of the country that it could plunge all local business into the most complete anarchy. The damage caused by those bankruptcies has been tremendous, because when you are confronted by those gangsters you feel insignificant, quite small and lost. Many citizens, lawyers and legal practitioners do not even want to have anything to do with those fraudulent bankruptcies because they fear for their lives.
Business is overrun to an outrageous extent by these crooks who rob us, ruin us, push us around and crush us. The fellow who purchases goods for next to nothing in these illegal bankruptcies makes enormous profits 23033-1141
Supply-Justice
because he can sell the goods at ridiculously low prices that defy competition. No store, no industry can compete against fraudulent bankruptcies.
The gang of crooks we think we know, Mr. Chairman, includes some respected and wealthy businessmen as well as professional crooks. They have found in this racket a unique opportunity to rob with maximum safety and respectability, because today fraudulent bankruptcies have become so perfect, so easy, I dare say even so legal, that one can emerge with barely a scratch.
Go out and see if you can find many fraudulent bankruptcy swindlers in prison; yet there are many in Canada. In my estimation, the bankruptcy racket is probably the safest and the most lucrative business at the present time.
They are definitely a gang of professionals familiar with every swindling trick. Most of them have a police record, and those who have not are no less dangerous; they may even be more dangerous because the police is not keeping as close a check on them as on the others and, consequently, they are more vulnerable.
They are wealthy; they own stores chocked full of goods from fraudulent bankruptcies. And their credit standing is good with all business and financial firms. They are shrewd; they belong to businessmen's organizations; they know a lot of people and have friends everywhere, even in clubs, hotels, credit offices, finance companies and banks.
They also have friends in the police force. They have legal advisers; they live in princely fashion in stylish apartments.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Businesses in a fix become the prey of those wise guys. They take advantage of it to make propositions to them. With their consent, they purchase those businesses and make them paying concerns within a few days. They deposit money in the bank, they pay cash for a certain time. Those people resort to every means to gain the confidence of manufacturers and suppliers.
Once the business has regained its good standing, they buy any type of merchandise and make it disappear at once. They build warehouses which burn down in a short time, and you can be sure, Mr. Chairman, that insurance companies have to pay tremendous amounts in insurance.
These people resort to all sorts of schemes. Their criminal minds make use of every imaginable means to fatten their fortunes.

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
I suppose the minister is beginning to realize that the Bankruptcy Act is a federal, not a provincial act. It is not up to the provincial government to amend the Bankruptcy Act.
Does the present act allow a person to go into bankruptcy? It does, because under the present system, it is impossible for quite a number for businessmen to avoid bankruptcy.
The system under which we are operating is financial nonsense. Those who benefit under the present system do so at the expense of others.
Our financial system, Mr. Chairman, is basically wrong. I ask the Minister of Justice to do all that is humanly possible to improve our economy and to prevent the series of fraudulent bankruptcies. Mr. Chairman, fraudulent bankruptcies lead to many others. This has created a disturbing situation in the province of Quebec and even in the whole country. I am speaking of the province of Quebec because I know of several of these bankruptcies and frauds there. I also know about some losses and all sorts of goings on. Those are terrible things, Mr. Chairman.
Therefore, I ask the honourable minister of Justice to punish those citizens as others have been punished. I know people who were sentenced to six months and even a year in jail for stealing $5 or $10. On the other hand, there are people who stole millions of dollars and were sentenced only to two or six months in jail. A person who steals but a small amount is punished much more severely than if he had stolen millions of dollars.
So, Mr. Chairman, because of this deplorable situation, I ask the Minister of Justice or his department to make the Bankruptcy Act inoperative. I ask him to close the door to all bankruptcies at this time, because there is no legislation, there are no rules to protect our citizens adequately, even from the standpoint of finance and human life.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Justice to padlock the Bankruptcy Act. I ask him to take this Act under his jurisdiction immediately, in order to take over all bankruptcies, fraudulent or otherwise, existing in Canada at the present time.
What the Minister of Justice must do is to actually give justice. We want justice in this matter. In the past three years, the federal government has done nothing in this regard. It is up to the federal government to intervene in those cases of fraudulent bankruptcies. We must put an end to those things and

the best way to do it is to make things secure by means of the padlock law, which has been used in many other circumstances. Let us use it with respect to the Bankruptcy Act and put some order in the economy of Canada and its provinces.
Let us give justice to families who have suffered from those murders. In the past five or six years, the criminals, the notorious bandits in question, have committed several murders for which we are indirectly responsible. It is time to settle this situation and I ask the Minister of Justice to restore some order in this field.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes this afternoon to make some comments regarding the report of the justice committee on juvenile delinquency in Canada. This is a very important matter and up to this time an opportunity has not arisen for comment in connection with the recently released report of that committee. I intend to indicate how I believe the house and the department should act on this report and I hope the result will be speedy action.
It seems to me from reading the report, Which is very lengthy and detailed running almost to 400 pages, that the committee has done a thorough and painstaking job regarding the methods of dealing with juvenile delinquency. Many of their suggestions are logical and could be put into effect quickly.
The report dealt particularly with methods of dealing with delinquency, which I believe that was the basic task of the committee. Certainly that is the major item covered by the committee's report. The committee did not attempt to deal with another aspect of delinquency relating to prevention and control, though it did make some suggestions as to what could be done along these lines.
I should like to mention some of the recommendations made by the committee as examples of the things that could be put into effect quickly without much difficulty to the department. The first is the suggestion that we set a minimum age of responsibility for juveniles at 10 or 12 years. This seems to be a logical and well-founded suggestion based on the evidence received by the committee. The committee recommends the establishment of a standard maximum age beyond which an individual is no longer considered a juvenile. The age suggested by the committee is 17, to be recognized across Canada. This also seems
February 25, 196S

to be a logical and reasonable conclusion reached as a result of the committee's inquiries.
We now have an unfortunate situation because in some provinces people are considered to be juveniles at 16 and in others the age is 18. This recommendation should cause very little difficulty. There are other recommendations such as permitting news media to attend juvenile court hearings. I think this is a good suggestion. The committee deals with the mechanics of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the method of dealing with juveniles themselves. The basic idea behind granting permission for news media to attend juvenile court hearings seems to be as much a case of providing a check on the juvenile court judges and the courts themselves as anything else. I think it is a very good idea.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
The field of juvenile delinquency is one in which very few are expert and these judges are appointed from all walks of life. Various courts are conducted in very different ways. I believe that while privacy of hearing is good for the child to the extent that no publicity ought to be given thereto, it can be very bad when judges use their own procedures and methods of dealing with people who are not represented by counsel and in many cases have not been formally charged. Therefore I believe that the recommendation that news media, including television and radio, be present at juvenile court hearings is a good one so long as the names of juveniles are withheld.
Another recommendation which could easily be adopted is that with regard to changes in nomenclature. The committee suggests changes in the words "delinquency" and "juvenile delinquents" and prefers the description "young offenders". I do not know that it matters a great deal and I am not too impressed with the conclusion in this regard, but if this is a general feeling there is certainly no objection to it.
There are a number of other recommendations such as requiring the presence of a juvenile's parents at a hearing. This is a good suggestion. I believe that in many cases parents who do not take the trouble to go to court when their children have been charged are themselves blameworthy and the judge should have the opportunity of dealing with them directly by discussion at the trial.
I think the recommendation to limit very severely the right of juvenile courts to commit children to a training school is a good
Supply-Justice
one, because in many cases it is too easy merely to get the child out of the way by sending him to a training school when you cannot think of any other solution. I believe the same situation exists in the adult courts and many people engaged in penology are now satisfied that too many people are committed and too little benefit comes from it.
The committee also investigated thoroughly the procedures which have grown up in the juvenile courts and I think they came to proper conclusions with regard to many of them. While the procedure in juvenile courts is of a very informal nature, judges are sometimes inclined to deal with the children who appear before them informally as well. By that I mean they often are inclined to assume children to be guilty until they prove themselves innocent.
Many of the suggestions the committee made were for the protection of the child in the juvenile court, making sure he is properly advised and represented, that any statements made are properly brought into evidence and that, while the penalty may not be too severe, before any conviction or finding of guilt is made it must be made on evidence. I think these suggestions are all valid.
There are some suggestions, however, that require more consideration. I should like to detail some of them and I think they should be considered by a committee and brought into effect as quickly as possible. The first recommendation that in my opinion causes some difficulty is the use of juvenile court records in adult courts and outside the courts. I believe the committee dealt with the question too loosely. It is my view that juvenlie court records should not be released to anyone except on the order of a judge who has already convicted a person in adult court. That is a matter of opinion but I believe it deserves consideration.
The committee suggested that a youth examiner system be investigated. They did not come to any conclusion in this respect. This system is in use in Israel and under it, instead of bringing young people into court as witnesses and in some cases even as defendants, a third person is entitled to discuss with the child the evidence he wishes to give and then give the evidence for the child. I believe this is an excellent suggestion and should be investigated. It has often been said that children are caused more harm than good in the courts, especially if they are very young and

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
are submitted to examination and crossexamination at an early age when they cannot form firm opinions on the various subjects put to them.
There is another matter that a committee of the house or some other body might inquire into. This concerns taking basically welfare matters completely out of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and dealing with them under provincial legislation. I understand that discussions are even now under way with provincial authorities in regard to this matter. The problem of delinquency as related to crime and the federal government's responsibility in criminal matters was in question in early years. It was felt when the Juvenile Delinquents Act was introduced that if a child was not to be classed as a criminal perhaps he should be dealt with under provincial welfare legislation. However, it was confirmed in the courts that the Juvenile Delinquents Act is a valid federal statute relating to federal responsibility for criminal matters and it has been dealt with on that basis.
I think the committee has wisely suggested that the time has come when the fringe elements which have been drawn into the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the juvenile courts ought to be removed. These are elements in which only the question of welfare is involved and not the commission of an offence. This is also a good recommendation and deserves consideration.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
I should now like to make some criticism of the report because, while it deals fully with the matter of handling juvenile delinquents, it has left virtually untouched a large field of problems concerning the prevention and control of juvenile delinquency. I do not say this in criticism of the committee because I do not believe it was set up to conduct an investigation into social welfare matters. The committee was made up of persons who basically were concerned with the methods rather than the social aspects of juvenile delinquency, and it recognized this in its report.
First, the committee found that statistics are not complete enough in order to come to conclusions on many of the social problems that are involved in juvenile delinquency and for that reason they were not able to come to such conclusions. Second, their second last recommendation suggested that demonstration projects under various aspects of delinquency prevention and control should be undertaken. I think that this was probably the

most important recommendation of the whole report because, while methods of dealing with juveniles can be changed, approaches altered and courts made more formal or less formal, these changes do not purport to deal with the cause and effect of delinquency and its prevention and control. Therefore, I believe this aspect requires a good deal more consideration than that given by the committee.
I suggest that some excellent work is being done in Ottawa and in many other cities in Canada in the social and welfare aspects of juvenile delinquency. But much more work of a pilot project nature is still required. For example, we find that while delinquency can be examined and dealt with in court and delinquents sent to training schools, in many cases the delinquents of today are the adult criminals of tomorrow. The success of the juvenile courts in dealing with young people foreshadows what will happen in the adult courts.
In the result, I should like to suggest that the reasonable and logical recommendations of the committee should be put into effect as quickly as possible; I think there is no problem there. The recommendations which require further study should be given that study and then implemented as quickly as possible.
The money required for pilot projects in delinquency prevention and control should be provided. I think we would all agree that criminal instincts or tendencies develop in a person's early years. Our penitentiaries are full of people who might have been valuable members of society had they been properly dealt with when they were young.
The cost of the penitentiaries branch and its administration is tremendous, as we can see from the estimates. The costs of administration of justice which are costs of the provinces are very great. We lose all across the line when a person becomes first a delinquent and subsequently a criminal. Society loses both financially and from a manpower and social point of view.
The starting place, Mr. Chairman, for criminals in this country, except those criminals we import, is at the juvenile age. We have to start with these young people, and I think that the report of this committee provides a good foundation for this.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to urge that, regardless of the method by which the recommendations of the committee are dealt with, recommendation No. 99 concerning the immediate establishment of pilot
February 25, 196$

projects in co-operation with the provincial authorities should be undertaken. Pilot projects are fairly easy to undertake, because they can be undertaken in a municipality or an area where real work is required and the results can be seen. Yesterday we saw that in the United States the administration is going to deal with the problem of water pollution by cleaning one river from source to mouth in one complete project. In that way they can eliminate everything which causes water pollution.
I should like to see this same approach to the problem of delinquency. I should like to see money put into certain areas to enable a complete job to be done which will also provide the foundation for similar work in other municipalities and areas of the country. I think that this recommendation is the most important one. The money used in implementing it will be well spent. It is only a drop in the bucket compared with what we spend in trying to apprehend, convict and incarcerate criminals in their later years. We have delayed too long.
The recommendations of the committee are not alarming. They find that the problem of juvenile gangs is not a serious one in Canada. They find that the main problem is damage to property, not damage to persons. They find that across the country many of the juveniles who are brought into court never return and that it is only the hard core cases which come back to the adult courts. For this reason I think we should make an immediate start to deal with our juvenile delinquents, and the best way to start is by employing the system of pilot projects recommended by the committee. I hope the government will give immediate consideration to setting up a pilot project or projects along this line and will either refer the remainder of the recommendations in the report to a parliamentary committee or take action on them in those fundamentals about which there is no disagreement.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in the discussion of these estimates, although I acknowledge that the Prime Minister himself remarked in his statement regarding the Spencer case that we could participate in a debate afterwards, I must emphasize that I rise in defence of civil liberties in this Canada of ours.
I have not been brought to my present convictions on the injustice that has been
Supply-Justice
meted out to Mr. Victor Spencer in Vancouver during the past several months by speeches which have been made in this House of Commons during the past few days. I have had this conviction ever since the month of November when I was advised that the Department of Justice had acted as judge, jury and executioner in the case without a hearing-when I say "hearing" I mean hearing; I do not mean a conversation with a senior official of the Civil Service Commission -without a hearing at which he could face his accuser, a hearing at which he could retain counsel on his own behalf.
I submit when the rights of one man, of one Canadian citizen are trampled upon in this country, the rights of all are trampled upon. I will not sit idly by and watch it being done.
I have to say with a heavy heart that I heard the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac state that the question of bankruptcies in the business world of Canada was ten times more important than the Spencer case. It makes me sad to think that there are members of the Canadian House of Commons who would place material gain before the individual free rights of native born and naturalized Canadian citizens.
In presenting his statement on Wednesday, February 23, the Prime Minister made this comment, as found on page 1681 of Hansard:
I know that the issues involved are important and I know that they have aroused very real uneasiness in the minds of hon. members.
I was very, very pleased to have the Prime Minister make this statement. He knows that it has aroused very real uneasiness in the minds of hon. members and I am one of those in whom very real uneasiness has been aroused.
On Wednesday night last we all had the opportunity of hearing the President of the United States in his 40 minute address discuss the problem of Viet Nam. It was a masterful presentation of the facts from his point of view. You may remember that during the course of his remarks he made an allusion to Macaulay who, when writing about Southey's "Colloquies", said "Men are never so likely to settle a question rightly as when they discuss it freely".
I should like to take part in a free discussion of the Spencer matter at this time.
Macaulay wrote and I repeat, "Men are never so likely to settle a question rightly as when they discuss it freely", and discussing it

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
freely does not consist of having a senior official of the Civil Service Commission journey out to Vancouver and speak to a junior civil servant with regard to some accusations which were levelled against him by people who did not give him an opportunity to meet his accusers in the courts of the land.
I was first elected to this house in June of
1962.	After ten months in opposition, following the 1963 election the Liberals took over the government seats. As I have listened to the inquiries being made of the cabinet whether or not a judicial inquiry had been authorized into this Spencer affair, as we have been calling it since November when the man was first identified by name, I began to wonder if this was not where I came in, in 1962. Everything seemed to be such a repetition of the answers that were given to the opposition in November of 1964 with regard to the Rivard affair, which was later investigated by Chief Justice Dorion of the Quebec Superior Court.
Over the past few weeks I have been reading all the Hansard transcripts of the discussions in this house dealing with the question of whether there should be an investigation into the 1964 allegations that employees in the federal government had been throwing offers of bribes round the halls of this building. The answers that were given at that time were the same as the answers being given with regard to this spencer matter when we ask, will there be a judicial investigation of the Spencer affair in order that the man may be able to clear his name before the Canadian public?
Last Wednesday we were told by the Prime Minister with regard to the Spencer affair that-and I quote:
Having studied all the facts of this case, I do not feel it is necessary or useful to initiate a judicial inquiry into this matter. The procedures that have been followed by the R.C.M.P. are exactly the same procedures that were followed when my right hon. friend was in the government.
If you turn to page 10397 of Hansard for November 23, 1964, you will find that the then minister of justice, in answer to questions being asked of him by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for the Yukon on the Rivard affair, said:
An inquiry was made immediately, upon my recommendation, into all aspects of this matter. When the inquiry was completed, the H.C.M. Police felt there was not sufficient evidence to recommend a prosecution.

This is the former minister of justice talking on November 23, 1964. Does that not sound like:
The procedures that have been followed by the R.C.M.P. are exactly the same procedures that were followed when my right hon. friend was in the government.
The then minister of justice continues on page 10379:
It was our joint assessment of the evidence that there was no case for the laying of information on the state of the evidence obtained.
Then he goes on:
As far as the minute details of the file, the names of witnesses and the persons interviewed are concerned, I am advised by the R.C.M. Police that this forms part of the contents of a report made by them which, as in the case of all reports of the R.C.M. Police to the minister, remains confidential in the public interest.
He then added:
I think it is also my duty to repeat to the committee that there has been an inquiry, and that the R.C.M. Police, the commissioner and myself, on an assessment of the whole evidence, do not feel or believe that there is sufficient evidence to justify the laying of information in the present state of the material obtained.
Now I quote from the Prime Minister's statement of last Wednesday:
However, before a final decision was taken to dismiss Mr. Spencer he was given a hearing by a senior official of the Civil Service Commission. Then we are told:
-neither at this hearing nor at those held by Canadian security officers-
That would be the R.C.M.P., of course.
Now we carry on to read the statement of the former minister of justice:
-it is not the practice of the R.C.M. Police or the Minister of Justice to refer matters to the law officers of the crown for opinions unless (a) the matter is brought to the attention of the minister for that purpose or (b) he is satisfied that there is room for opinion. There has not been a formal submission to the law officers of the crown in this case.
He is referring to the fact that the R.C.M.P. had made a definite statement to him. According to this report there was not sufficient evidence to recommend prosecution in the Rivard matter. We were told in the statement by the Prime Minister last Wednesday that there was not sufficient evidence produced to justify a prosecution in the Spencer case. On November 23, 1964, page 10397, we were told:
-it is not the practice of the R.C.M. Police or the Minister of Justice to refer matters to the law officers of the crown for opinions unless-there is room for opinion.
I do not know whether or not that means a difference of opinion. I continue quoting:
-he is satisfied that there is room for opinion. There has not been a formal submission to the law officers of the crown in this case.
February 25, 1966

We are told in the matter of Spencer that the law officers of the Crown had advised against instituting criminal proceedings against Mr. Spencer and that proceedings were not taken. From that we can judge that there was room for a difference of opinion and that a reference was made to the law officers of the Crown. This is very interesting. I would like to see the papers on the matter. I took part, in opposition, in discussions on motions for production of papers with regard to the levy of tariffs by the former government. I was told that these papers are confidential.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
It is interesting to find that in one case the former Minister of Justice tells us he did not refer the matter to the law officers of the Crown because he did not think there would be room for opinion. This time we find there has been such a reference and we were told no action would be taken in the form of a judicial inquiry. We know what happened in the previous case of 1964. There was a judicial inquiry and much came out of that inquiry which would never have been adduced if there had merely been acceptance of the statement of the then minister of justice. Why should we believe there is nothing to be brought forward in favour of Spencer at this time just because we are told it is not necessary or useful to initiate a judicial inquiry into this matter?
I would not be speaking this way with regard to civil liberties if I were not greatly upset by the fact that a minister of the Crown in a nation-wide television broadcast had named this man. If ever a man was accused without having an opportunity to speak on his own behalf, this was the occasion. They argue that his name was already known because he had disclosed it to a newspaper reporter who had interviewed him. But how could his name be kept unknown in the city in which he worked when it was realized he was no longer in the service of the Post Office Department where he had been employed for some time? His fellow workers were well aware he had been removed from his employment and they were naturally curious that a 57-year-old man should be removed. Without doubt there was talk in the Vancouver post office and in the city of Vancouver about this man's disappearance from the federal service. But it was altogether improper, unjust and indefensible for a minister of the Crown to go on the air over a national television network and name 23033-115
Supply-Justice
the man involved in the case even though he himself had said in a statement made in the fall of last year: "I must be the man involved".
This man is entitled to a full and complete hearing. If it must be held in camera I would have no objection. But to condemn him to a life under surveillance, to remove his pension rights and to fire him without due process of law is contrary to all the principles of-dare I say British justice or must I say "Canadian justice"? When the red ensign was hauled down in the spring of 1965 in this country we did not expect to see the enforcement of British principles of justice go out the window the following winter. I myself will fight for the maintenance of the great principles of British justice-I will call it Canadian justice if you wish-but if this man is not given a hearing I will not have much respect for Canadian justice. I will still fight for British justice.
He is entitled to a hearing. He is entitled to face his accusers personally. Whether or not such a hearing is held in public I do not care provided it is before a third party who is objective in every sense of the word. I do not believe that a man who has had an opportunity of speaking only to a senior officer of the Civil Service Commission and to Canadian security officers has been given a just and proper hearing or one which justifies removing him from his job.
I ask this question: Would they be able to separate this man from his income had he been working for anybody other than the federal government? What would his position have been had he been working in the mines or for the Pacific Great Eastern Railway or for some of the big fruit growing companies of British Columbia? I suggest it would not have been a simple matter to have separated him from his position in those circumstances, because he had never been tried or accused in open court. I say that the defence of the civil liberties of the individual is the first burden which should rest on every member of the House of Commons no matter on what side he sits.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
There are some amazing coincidences in the cases of Rivard and Spencer. I referred to one of these the other day in conversation with an hon. member. It had to do with a discussion whether someone had said "heads will roll" or "heads will swim".
One hon. member read a newspaper clipping and it turned out that Mr. Spencer had

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
said "Heads will swim". Now hon. members will find that very expression used as recorded in Hansard of November 23, 1964 at page 10387 at the bottom of the column. The hon. member for Yukon was speaking and he said:
I feel that If such an offence had been made by anyone other than Mr. Denis, charges would have been laid so fast it would have made his head swim.
I do not know why these coincidences occur. I begin to think this is where I came in. When I hear of these objections to a judicial inquiry with regard to the Spencer affair, all I need do is change the name to Rivard in order to hear exactly the same record-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: And change the Minister of Justice too. The same old tune.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Anyway, what was done in this case was very different from the treatment handed out to Mr. Belec and Mr. Poi-tras. These are two gentlemen from the city of Montreal who were employees of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. What happened in this case? We have not been given full official details of what occurred but from a press release we understand that certain moneys were unaccounted for and that these funds were under the control of the two men I have mentioned. A court was held to decide this matter. I say "a court" because under the appropriate act dealing with the R.C.M.P. this parliament has given authority to the R.C.M.P. to make certain arrangements to deal with internal discipline. A court was held to investigate the accusations brought against these two highly placed officers of the force. One of them, an inspector in the province of Quebec, is the only commissioned officer in the 98 years of history of the R.C.M.P. to be convicted of a crime in the R.C.M.P. courts.
The R.C.M.P. brought in one of its senior men from Edmonton and a just hearing was held. These two men were brought before the hearing. They then appealed the verdict handed down by this official from Edmonton. The appeal went before the commissioner and was referred to a review board. The appeal board gave its verdict and delivered it to the commissioner. We understand that the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. wished to dismiss summarily these two highly placed officers of the R.C.M.P. working in the province of Quebec in the city of Montreal.
What happened? The matter was referred to the cabinet before any such drastic step was taken. It affected pension rights. After

many months of probing and inquiring we came up with the facts to which I have referred earlier in this house. I spoke on this question at some length on June 30, 1965. I have here copies of the orders in council in which these men who had been found guilty by a properly constituted court of failing to account properly for funds placed under their control were retired. They were anxious to retain their pension rights.
The cabinet goes to work and considers the many years of fine service these men gave up to the time the defalcations were discovered, and by special order in council Chief Superintendent Rene John Belec was compulsorily retired from the R.C.M.P. on a pension of $6,624 per annum.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Where was Mr. Spencer then? He was a junior clerk in the Vancouver post office and had no access to secret or confidential papers.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Yet at the same time the Treasury Board, approved by His Excellency the Governor General in Council, recommended that:
Sub-Inspector Joseph Hosanna Maurice Poitras, who was compulsorily retired from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force-
Be paid a pension
-at the rate of $1,526.80 per annum from December 9, 1964, until such date as he attains the age of 65 years and thereafter at the rate of $1,953.30 per annum.
These two men were given a trial by the properly constituted court of internal discipline of the R.C.M.P. They appealed and the verdict of the appeal court was referred to the cabinet with this result.
What about Mr. Spencer? We know he has had no open trial. We know he was not before any properly constituted court. Where is his pension? Gone with the wind. Where is his job? Gone with the wind. The man can whistle for his welfare and future so far as the Prime Minister's actions are concerned. I maintain that there has to be an investigation into the matters concerning this affair.
How can we say that two representatives of a great foreign power were engaged in certain espionage activities and therefore should be asked to leave the country and then turn around and say, "We cannot prove it with regard to the man they were supposed to be dealing with; there is not sufficient evidence on which to obtain a conviction"? If we cannot prove that the Canadian citizen was cooperating with these representatives of a
February 25, 1966

18C9
foreign power, then the foreign power should be asked to send back its two representatives to Canada.
I say you cannot have it two ways. I say you cannot condemn people and tell them, "You must leave the country", and then say to our own citizen, "We cannot hang anything on you so we will just place you under surveillance, remove your pension rights, take you off your job, but we are not able to secure a conviction in open court. The security officials who have investigated the matter have said so".
We are trampling on the rights of every Canadian when we take that action with regard to this man Spencer in Vancouver, and I ask that we have a judicial investigation by a third party, in camera if you will but a third party who will enjoy the confidence of every member of the House of Commons.
Referring again to the opening days of the Rivard affair-I do not think I missed a moment in the House of Commons while the session was going on-on November 23, 1964, as recorded at page 10386 of Hansard, the then minister of justice said:
The reason I personally have decided that until further evidence were obtained it would not be fair to lay a charge is only because the laying of charges in a case where one knows there is no chance of judicial success is an act of smear, a lack of charity and an injustice-
If in the present case I had personally ordered the laying of a charge, I would have betrayed my conscience and acted against the principle that would govern an honest citizen, because I might have brought about the condemnation without trial .... of two young men whose future ought not to be placed in jeopardy-*
The minister of justice of that day stated:
If in the present case I had personally ordered the laying of a charge I would have betrayed my conscience and acted against the principle that would govern an honest citizen, because I might have brought about the condemnation without trial .... of two young men-
That being so, what does one say about a minister of justice who appears on a national television network and makes the statement, accusing a person who has had no opportunity of a legitimate trial, that he has been participating in espionage activities? I say, Mr. Chairman, you cannot have it two ways.
I have another interesting report, again one of these repetitious pieces that I would like to put on the record. In 1964, again on November 23, as recorded at page 10,391 of Hansard the then minister of justice stated:
-A full report was made to me and discussed with the commissioner on September 18 of this year. I do not want to mislead the house and give 23033-1151
Supply-Justice
the impression that the commissioner has made a decision. It was not up to the commissioner to decide. We discussed his views on the matter from the standpoint of police investigation and fact finding as a result of the investigation. With regard to any decision respecting the lodging of a complaint in the light of the report and that conversation, I, of course, must take responsibility because under the statute the legal adviser to the crown is the Minister of Justice, and not the commissioner of the R.C.M.P.-
In the statement made by the Prime Minister on Wednesday we are told that it is not necessary or useful to initiate a judicial inquiry.
The procedures that have been followed by the R.C.M.P. are exactly the same procedures that were followed when my right hon. friend was in the government.
We are also told that Mr. Spencer did not protest at the hearing held by Canadian security officers, which would be the R.CM.P., and that the R.C.M.P. again advised the present Minister of Justice that an action for criminal proceedings would not bring a conviction. Speaking of the word "conviction", I have here in my hand a copy of the Official Secrets Act of the Dominion of Canada chapter 198 of the statutes. In section 14(1) we read:
For the purposes of the trial of a person for an offence under this act-
Well, that is very nice. It says:
For the purposes of the trial of a person for an offence under this act-
Suppose you do not have a trial under the act? I guess this would not apply but we are told Spencer was violating the Official Secrets Act. When this act was passed in 1939 it is a certainty that the government intended that anybody accused of an offence under it should get a trial. That is why it says:
For the purposes of the trial-
It does not say trial by a representative of the Civil Service Commission or by a security officer of the crown.
Section 15(1) says:
Where no specific penalty is provided in this act, any person who is guilty of an offence under this act shall be deemed to be guilty of an indictable offence and is, on conviction, punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years;-
I am not quarreling with the Official Secrets Act but I should like to see it enforced. I do not want to see it evaded because every evasion of the law of the land simply sets a precedent for further evasions in further aspects of the law. I quote again section 14(1) which says:
For the purposes of the trial of a person for an offence under this act-

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
And section 15(1) which says:
Where no specific penalty is provided in this act, any person who is guilty of an offence under this act shall be deemed to be guilty of an indictable offence and is, on conviction, punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.
There has been no trial in the case of Spencer so how could there be a conviction?
I have been reading about the similarities between the Spencer affair and the Belec and Poitras case because of the pension angle and because of the Rivard affair. Only yesterday I read the comments of the hon. member for Athabasca, as recorded at page 2562 of Hansard for June 17, 1965. He is a former member of the R.C.M.P. with 23 years service in the R.C.M.P. and the Canadian army and this is what he said on that occasion:
The Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is in a very unenviable position. On the one hand, he is permitted to exercise almost unlimited discretion and in certain cases the government is willing to stake its reputation and its whole future on his judgment. On the other hand, other decisions made by the same man are either completely ignored or overridden. I suggest that you cannot have it both ways.
In the case of Belec and Poitras the R.C.M.P. recommended that they be dismissed but these two men went to the cabinet and one of them was given a very handsome pension and the other a worth-while pension. In this case the R.C.M.P. report was overridden. In the case of the Rivard inquiry we were told that the R.C.M.P. maintained that no convictions could be obtained if charges were laid, but look at what the situation is today when this matter is pressed?
We are told again in the Spencer case that it would be impossible to convict Mr. Spencer if charges were laid on the present evidence. I say that Mr. Spencer must be given his day in court even if it is in camera before a judge of the highest courts of this land or before a small committee of the House of Commons. I do not object to the inquiry being in camera but I would like to see the judge a third party, not someone directly interested in this matter.
There is much that can be said about this matter. I could bring in the Landreville case.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
People are running around telling us we must not condemn him without trial, this is not fair, this is against Canadian justice, people are making accusations against Mr. Justice Landreville and he has no opportunity to answer them. What about Mr. Spencer? He is just a little fellow from Vancouver but
[Mr. Cowan.)
Mr. Justice Landreville, in terms of the street, is a big shot. He was mayor of Sudbury. He has appealed his income tax assessments to the Tax Appeal Board because they were so heavy. He is a member of the Supreme Court of Ontario. We are told, do not pre-judge the case, apply British justice and fair play. I say if that is the argument they are going to use with Mr. Justice Landreville, and I believe in his being given justice and fair play-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member for York-Humber has expired.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr, Chairman, before coming to the house in early January, I had, on many occasions and like most Canadians, read press reports about the Victor Spencer case. Since I have been sitting here, that is, since January 18, I have heard this name spoken much more frequently than that of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) or of the leader of the government (Mr. Pearson).
I have heard the name of Victor Spencer repeatedly, much more often than I heard members of the house propose pieces of legislation beneficial to the Canadian people.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that parliament is a place to speak one's mind and that the duty of an opposition is to oppose. However, I believe there are reasonable limits beyond which one cannot step without being discredited before the public opinion. In fact, I know that public opinion is getting fed up with these useless discussions that serve only to obstruct government business. Yet, the opposition continues to talk of the Spencer case with an enthusiasm worthy of the best causes.
I have the feeling that Mr. Spencer's defenders speak on his behalf with more ardour, conviction and devotion than they would to defend Her Majesty the Queen of England, the integrity of Canada or the freedom of a citizen wrongly imprisoned.
What is this all about? Involved is a citizen who, we have serious reasons to believe, took part in seditious or dangerous activities against this country, who acted treasonably toward his country in favour of a foreign power.
I realize that the opposition is entitled to ask questions, as I said before, but this has got to stop somewhere. The opposition is justified in suspecting that something fishy is
February 25, 196G

going on in high places. I know that the opposition is justified, in each case, in invoking the rights of man.
What I do not understand is when members take advantage of this to keep harping on the Rivard case, Banks and Doctor Mar-coux. All those things have been settled either by the courts or by inquiries. At any rate they were settled last year during the last election campaign, when the federal government had the opportunity to examine its conscience and consider the penance imposed by public opinion, since it was deprived of the strong majority it was seeking.
I think that these things should be considered settled and the Canadian people given the legislation for which they are waiting.
Let us return to the Spencer case. I think that the government must have found some extenuating circumstances to proceed as it did. Everyone knows that it is not always easy to establish legal evidence. But when national security is involved, the government is entitled to take certain precautions, because this becomes a matter of the public good.
When speaking of human rights, there is a distinction to be made, since public good has priority over private interest. This should be remembered in relation to the present case.
I am told that Mr. Spencer confessed. I agree with the opposition that the government should not have taken his pension away; in my opinion, the government should have given it back to him. It belongs to him; he must live, as well as his family, even if he took part in seditious activities.
I do not want to speak very long, Mr. Chairman, because it would be illogical. In view of the remarks I wanted to make, I would like to propose a compromise. Everything that is being said leads to what? Are we trying to make a martyr out of Mr. Spencer for his various supporters? That seems obvious to those who, like me, do not belong to any party.
What is being achieved? Parliament is paralysed, the people who are expecting a constructive legislative program are paying the price of that debate, and Mr. Spencer has been pilloried.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would like to propose a compromise:	the government
should, in the circumstances, agree to hold a judicial inquiry in camera as soon as possible, if the opposition will agree not to obstruct any longer business of the house by coming
Supply-Justice
back all the time to the Rivard, Marcoux and Hal Banks cases.
We are considering estimates covering money already spent. We will have the opportunity to come back to those matters and we should try to come to a truce. A very successful effort was made last night, and I think the persons responsible for this deserve congratulations, so that the legislative program that the people are anxiously awaiting may finally be introduced.
Changes were made within the cabinet; the responsibilities of individual ministers were redistributed also. We know that the members of the cabinet are planning the legislative program that the people are clamouring for. If some people keep on staging filibusters on matters such as the Spencer case, we will never do any constructive work.
Let us not forget that there are more important matters than the Spencer case. The sick are waiting for the health insurance scheme; the unemployed are waiting for legislation to get work; in business men are waiting for the economy to improve; old people are waiting for a pension fund. And we spend weeks and weeks discussing matters already settled.
In spite of the importance of individual rights, I maintain that those matters are more important than the Spencer case.
I should like to suggest once again this compromise that should be acceptable both to the opposition and to the government: let the government, in a gesture of self-denial, agree to a confidential judicial inquiry, since state secrets and national security are involved to a certain extent, and let the opposition agree to stop harping on the same old stories, such as the Dorion inquiry, the Rivard case and so on. I am shocked to see the Prime Minister who, after all, with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) is responsible for the administration of the country, compelled to prevent a greater evil by setting up a surveillance such as the one to which was submitted this individual accused of spying.
I am surprised to see that the Prime Minister is being attacked not only by the members opposite but that even some of his friends are taking pot shots at him from the rear and compare cases in no way similar since the case of Mr. Belec of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has no point of comparison with Mr. Spencer's case. The latter is a traitor to his country whereas the former and his compatriot spent a lifetime defending their country. The charge laid

February 25. 1966
Supply-Justice
against them was a very light one and if the government was harsh on them, it is because they were police officers who cannot be allowed even the smallest peccadillos.
The Canadian people will not be happy with the discussion going on around the name of Spencer. What is required is a legislative program to meet the needs of the people. They are fed up with these insignificant and endless discussions. As an independent member, wishing to take neither side, I would suggest that both sides meet half-way. Let the government immediately agree to this in camera judicial inquiry and let the opposition put an end to this nonsense and let us get on with constructive legislation.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to deal very briefly with the Spencer case but before doing so I should like to inform the Minister of Justice that it is my intention to discuss bankruptcy frauds in general. I am going to leave specifics aside until question No. 577 on the order paper has been answered. It is one which sets forth some very pertinent questions to be answered by the ministry. If the Minister of Justice is prepared to answer those questions during the course of our consideration of his estimates on Monday I will be pleased to follow him in making my remarks about this subject. In any event, I want to have those answers before I engage in any specifics regarding bankruptcy frauds.
At this time I want to deal very briefly with the Prime Minister's statement of February 23 wherein he stated, as recorded at page 1682 of Hansard and as repeated by the hon. member for York-Humber this afternoon, that at no time did any spokesman of the government identify Spencer. That is simply not true. Mr. Spencer was approached by a Vancouver reporter, Tom Hazlitt of the Vancouver Province. Mr. Spencer identified himself to Mr. Hazlitt but Mr. Hazlitt kept that information in confidence. It was the Minister of Justice himself who on a television broadcast first mentioned the name of Mr. Spencer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: I am sure the minister will recall that that is the case if he searches his memory carefully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is not the case.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
The minister will have to satisfy me and a good many other members of this house to the contrary. The hon. member for York-Humber put his finger on the 
situation and he is a member of the minister's own party. The leader of the New Democratic Party skirted the fringes of the real facts in this case. Whatever the minister says, the fact remains that Mr. Spencer's name was first mentioned by him to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is not a fact.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: He did so on a television broadcast. Before leaving that matter I join with those who demand that an in camera inquiry be held in order to determine whether or not there was sufficient evidence upon which Mr. Spencer was dismissed and denied his pension rights. The minister is following exactly the same wrong course followed by his predecessor, acting as the prosecutor-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That was the Leader of the Opposition.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I will have something to say about the Leader of the Opposition vis-a-vis the Minister of Justice in a moment or so. The Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister have acted as chief prosecutor, judge and lord high executioner in the most arrogant and unjust way possible, in precisely the same way as the former minister of justice acted regarding other matters that have already been discussed in this house.
The Prime Minister in his statement of February 23 said:
The law officers of the Crown had advised against instituting criminal proceedings against Mr. Spencer-
Why is that so? What is being covered up? Mr. Spencer said that heads will swim. Whose heads, and why will they swim? These are very pregnant questions which are being left unanswered. If proceedings should be taken against others, if there have been offences of which Mr. Spencer could inform us then these would come out before an independent judge or commissioner sitting to ascertain the facts, not only with regard to whether justice is being done in this case but in others as well.
If evidence does not exist upon which proceedings could be taken against Spencer then why was he dismissed and why was he denied pension rights? If evidence did exist upon which proceedings could be taken, why were they not taken? If, as the Prime Minister said in his statement, much of the evidence would be inadmissible in a court of law, what is the danger of taking proceedings, because that evidence would be inadmissible in any event? Who is the Prime Minister to set himself as the arbiter of what is or is not admissible evidence?
February 25, 1966

Members have already dealt with the Hal Banks case. The hon. member tor Verdun in a posturing manner criticized the previous government for its conduct in dealing with the Banks matter. Last session when the Industrial Relations Committee was sitting I tried day after day to place evidence before that committee but I was prevented from doing so by a majority comprised of Liberal members, of which the present Minister of Agriculture was the chief spokesman.
That information was made available to law enforcement officers in this country and the books of the S.I.U. were seized. Unless I miss my guess, there will be sufficient evidence upon which to base extraditable charges against the elusive Mr. Banks. The Liberal Party had a majority on the Industrial Relations Committee the last time it sat and they were supported by our friends to the left. I am surprised to note that the hon. member for Winnipeg North has called for the production of the Norris working papers, because his party supported the Liberal objection to the introduction of this evidence before the Industrial Relations Committee the last time it sat.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: The Liberals did not have a majority.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: They did when supported by our friends to the left, as they do today with that same support.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: I am just trying to help you get your facts straight.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: My facts are usually borne out. We now have a Minister of Justice telling us, as he told us last fall and as he told the press when the matter of the Sefkind bankruptcy files came up, that he has no responsibility in this field. He invited the Leader of the Opposition to peruse those files but would have nothing to do with my request to look at them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: That is right. You are not a privy councillor, are you?

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: He said there was no responsibility and it was not a federal matter at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: What are you quoting?

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
He said it was a matter that concerned only the province. He said that again in his own official press release of September 9, 1965, which has not yet been quoted verbatim to him.
It is of interest today to consider some of the words the Minister of Justice used in this
Supply-Justice
press release which was issued by the minister in connection with accusations made by Mr. Kierans of Quebec when he was the revenue minister. He suggested that the federal Department of Justice was being negligent and indifferent in the administration of the Bankruptcy Act. Mr. Kierans charged the justice department with "considerably hindering" the Quebec war against the underworld and demanded that the new justice minister, the one who sits before the committee this afternoon, tighten up on bankruptcy controls in the light of the Mercier commission report made public last month.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
What did the minister say in his press release of September 9, 1965?

Since that time there has been a steady increase in the development of organized criminal groups in Canada, composed of both local criminals and of those foreign criminals who have managed to settle in this country.
From Canada, these groups maintain a close working relationship and personal tie with many of the U.S.A. based syndicates, and it is significant that many of these U.S.A. groups have recently been labelled as "Mafia" by the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Organized Crime. The Canadian groups also maintain connections with criminal elements in Southern Italy and Sicily, which the Italian authorities call "Mafiosa", and with criminals in other urban areas of Canada where the commercial development and high population density offers potentially fertile breeding grounds for development of lucrative crime.
We find these groups at present centred mainly in the more densely populated commercially developed areas of Ontario and Quebec. Their criminal activities fluctuate into nearly all fields of lucrative crime. We find them active in such things as extortion rackets, stock frauds, gambling, labour racketeering, narcotics, counterfeiting, bankruptcy fraud, illicit liquor, arson fraud, business manipulation and other forms of racketeering.
These groups have over the years developed a fairly efficient and well organized administrative system-
