speechtext: I do not mind answering that question very briefly. My view is that the war against organized crime must be given national direction. This can only be done by clothing a national police force with the authority to operate in an organized way, and provincial authorities must co-operate to the extent necessary to make this possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
One of the matters which is of the greatest concern to us in these estimates is that raised by members of the Official Opposition and supported by members of the New Democratic party with respect to what is now called the Spencer case.
I believe one question which should be answered is this: Who dismissed Spencer? My understanding is that it was the Civil Service Commission, an agency not responsible to government. If Spencer has been deprived of his pension rights it is because the Civil Service Commission is convinced that, in light of all the circumstances, this is the proper course to take. If the commission was not satisfied after their inquiry, what about the 11,000 postal workers? They have not always been silent recently, but their silence in this particular case is eloquent. I submit that these loyal Canadians recognize subversion and dissociate themselves from it.
We should ask ourselves here-because the public may not be clear on this: What precisely are the provisions under which this man's employment was terminated? I refer
February 25, 1966

hon. members to section 50 of the Civil Service Act which is as follows:
(1)	The tenure of office of an employee is during the pleasure of Her Majesty, subject to the provisions of this and any other Act and the regulations thereunder, and unless some other period of employment is specified, for an indeterminate period.
(2)	Nothing in this Act shall be construed to limit or affect the right or power of the Governor in Council to remove or dismiss any employee.
In case Canadians may wonder whether this is something weird and wonderful and new, I think it might be useful to refer to the debate which took place on September 19, 1961 concerning clause 50 which deals with tenure of office. I read from Hansard of that date at page 8576.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 50 introduces something which is extremely peculiar. Section 50(1) reads as follows:
The tenure of office of an employee is during the pleasure of Her Majesty, subject to the provisions of this and any other act and the regulations thereunder, and, unless some other period of employment is specified, for an indeterminate period.
Later he says:
I therefore move that clause 50 be amended by the deletion of subclause (2).
The hon. member for Carleton, the responsible minister, made this contribution, in part:
This particular subclause is merely a preservation of the over-all prerogative of the crown. It is in the existing act and it was never repealed.
Later he went on to say:
I think it is significant that the maintenance in this bill of this particular subclause which the hon. member seeks to delete was approved by all three members of the civil service commission who appeared before the special committee as witnesses. It is also significant that no representations of any kind were made in relation to it by any of the civil service staff associations. I think the hon. member is well aware of how carefully in clause 60 new provisions have been set forth dealing with dismissals and the right of appeal. This particular provision merely preserves the over-all prerogative of the Crown, one which I am sure will not at any time be abused. In view of this I shall ask the committee to reject the amendment.
My hon. friend from Ottawa West, now Minister of Public Works and leader of the house, whom I acknowledge as one of the most competent, experienced and wise persons on matters of government from the opposition bench made this interjection:
The subclause as it now stands reads:
2. Nothing in this act shall be construed to limit or affect the right or power of the governor in council to remove or dismiss any employee.
This appears on first reading to be very wide in its language and undoubtedly it is but I do not see any way of restricting that right-
Supply-Justice
He is speaking of the right of the governor in council to dismiss on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
It seems to me that a government has to be held responsible for the administration and the discharge of its duties and that in line with that responsibility there must be this power of dismissal.
Later, he added:
I recall a situation which developed in this country some 15 years ago in which this power was of real value to a government.
We all remember what happened 15 years earlier-the Gouzenko inquiry. I regard the exchange which I have just read as being one typical of two experienced lawyers, well versed in matters of parliament and with a thorough knowledge of the interests of the civil service. They are agreed that there must be some exceptions. I listened with interest to the speech made by the hon. member for York South. I am prepared to accept at its face value the observations made by the Prime Minister when he said:
I have examined this situation personally. I have studied all the reports, all the documents concerning this case. I have spent a good many hours, Mr. Chairman, in doing so because I know that the issues involved are important.
I accept what he says finally, by way of conclusion:
I believe Mr. Spencer's dismissal and his loss of pension rights under the law was lawful and just. I do not believe his rights as a person or as a citizen have been violated. On the contrary, I believe he has been treated with scrupulous fairness.
May I say with the utmost sincerity that had those words been spoken by the Leader of the Official Opposition or by any minister charged with this responsibility I would have accepted them as meaning precisely what they said.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Is he saying that section 50 of the Civil Service Act means that the governor in council has the right to dismiss arbitrarily without cause and without ever having to account for his actions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I think it is clear that section 50 provides no limitation to the right or power of the governor in council to remove or dismiss any employee. The usual dismissal section of the act is of course section 60 which provides for notice of dismissal, the right of appeal and so on. Subsection 4 provides for cases where there is an appeal.
Supply-Justice

February 25, 1966
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Subsection 5, by way of conclusion, provides that the governor in council may dismiss an employee pursuant to a recommendation under this section. What I am saying is that section 50 is an extraordinary section. I believe section 50 is important for the security of Canada. I most seriously care about this matter and I believe the Prime Minister and those charged with the preservation of security in this country care about it too.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: So do all hon. members. Do not arrogate to yourself that monopoly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Perhaps by way of reply I might simply say that I have here an editorial which appeared in the Christian Century of February 22, 1933 under the heading, "Communism Knows There is a Revolution." I believe that what is said in that editorial spells out exactly what is happening today. It may be that my hon. friend from York South does not agree, but I believe that there is a great power contest in the world, and Canada would like to see this power contest cease. We would be very happy if the confrontation could be avoided. Obviously persons who are protagonists in it are good customers and we would like to have them as good friends. I am referring not only to the Russians but also to the Chinese, and I think our external, as well as trade and commerce policies must be directed towards the end of bridging divisions in every conceivable fashion. But we are not blind, we recognize there is an ideological contest of vast proportions and that Canada, by virtue of its friendly relationship to the United States is being subjected to the most powerful propaganda campaign at this particular time. Of course, as was said we had difficulties in 1946 and no doubt pressure will continue. It is the duty of the Minister of Justice, mindful of the great burden of preserving civil liberty, to be also mindful of the preservation and security of the nation; and that preservation and security is a first responsibility of government.
Since I became a member of the house in 1961, far too often have I heard the R.C.M.P. pulled down and derided by people in the house and outside it. I believe Canadians owe an enormous debt to these people who, in many instances, remain silent, do their work for the security of all of us, and oft times are underpaid and understaffed. This is a force the activities of which are spread over the saving of lives, maritime patrol, traffic control, surveillance over narcotics,-indeed, covering a very wide range of fields. The fact 
that with so little offence, they have been able to accomplish so much in the security field, when we are right in the centre of a confrontation between forces, communist and west, is quite remarkable.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to indicate how the security of Canada would be endangered if there were an inquiry into the matter, by a judge or some other person, held in camera, and the result of that inquiry presented to the house and the country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: I think there are certain facts in this case not known to my hon. friend and not likely ever to be known.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: And which would not be known if the inquiry were held in camera.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not want to dilate on this point at length. We have taken a position which can easily be characterized as unpopular. However, I think it has been a responsible decision after weighty consideration of all the facts. It is not a popular decision but I would like to think we will be supported in it, just as we would support the right hon. gentleman opposite if he were faced with this problem. I think there are more things in this chamber upon which to join forces than to cause differences.
I wish now to touch on the charge of bifurcation or trifurcation of the Department of Justice. I do so because, frankly, for years I have felt that the Department of Justice was a very overloaded portfolio in the Canadian government. This was a department that called for a variety of responsibilities, in some cases responsibilities which conflicted with each other.
May I briefly summarize some of the responsibilities of the Minister of Justice before the reorganization.
1.	To administer a large department charged with the responsibility of advising all other departments of government.
2.	To advise as to legislation.
3.	To recommend as to judicial and quasilegal appointments.
4.	To advise as to constitutional change, and to advise concerning highly complex dominion-provincial relations.
5.	To administer this vast quasi-military force, the R.C.M.P., with all its diverse duties, spread across 3,000 miles of country.
6.	To administer the penitentiary service.
7.	To administer the parole service.
8.	To administer anti-combines legislation.
February 25, 1966

9.	To administer bankruptcy legislation.
If we look at this work in comparison with Ontario or the United Kingdom it shows that what has been attempted in the past is far too much for any one minister. Duties which in England would be covered through the home office, the attorney general and the solicitor general were all combined under one minister in Canada. The province of Ontario has its attorney general, a minister of reform institutions and a provincial secretary. Indeed, Ontario is presently discussing appointment of a solicitor general. I cannot help feeling that no minister of justice, because of the weight and variety of his duties, has been able to give any substantial consideration to more than one or another of these many responsibilities.
I would point out these facts, that since the final tabling of the Fauteux committee report, which you will remember was the result of the efforts of Hon. Stuart Garson and his letter of December 11, 1953, the report being dated April 30, 1956, we had as minister of justice Hon. Stuart Garson for 417 days, Hon. Davie Fulton for 1,875 days, Hon. Donald Fleming for 257 days, Hon. Lionel Chevrier for 287 days, Hon. Guy Favreau for 513 days, and Hon. Lucien Cardin for 163 days.
The point I am making is that with the complexity of these responsibilities I do not believe we have ever had a minister of justice who truly got on top of the full variety of these responsibilities.
While it may not logically satisfy all requirements I think there is a certain harmony in putting the R.C.M.P., the penitentiary service and the parole service in one packet.
This is not inconsistent with the British experience and practice. I believe the splitting of the department shows serious evidence of the concern of the government with respect to all the problems we have heard discussed today, on the one hand problems of security, and on the other hand problems of economic supervision and control.
In this latter connection I am thinking of fraudulent bankruptcy and combines legislation-legislation which, in its character, is essentially economic-
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
One subject that is of most concern to me-and this is because of interests I have had over 15 or 20 years-is improvement and development with regard to the field of penology. I have read carefully, after hearing it, the address of the Solicitor General. It was
Supply-Justice
modest, it was factual, and as usual for him gracious in all its utterances. But to me it is eloquent in what it does not say. As you will remember, the Solicitor General in reporting to this house spoke of the size of our prison population, the overcrowding of institutions, the great need for more research in criminology, and the problem of Staff recruitment. I was disappointed, if he will forgive me, in what he said in respect of the building program. Personally I have been anxious in respect of this building program. The minister told us that during the next eight months five new medium security institutions will be opened at Springhill, Cowansville, Wark-worth, Drumheller and Matsqui, the costs of which would be $40 million. I can tell the Solicitor General that there are many people who are interested in criminology and penological science who are concerned about the character of some of these proposed buildings.
Personally I think we have made some serious mistakes. I think Matsqui is a gross mistake, but also that it is an honest mistake where Canada has attempted to do something. When I look over to my hon. friend for Bow River I think that Drumheller, for many reasons, is a mistake.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Have you ever been to Drumheller?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Then how can you say that it is a mistake?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Because it is so hard to get there is one reason you should not put an institution in that place.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Hard to get there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: How silly can you get.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: May I make this observation that the penitentiary at Drumheller, Alberta is being built in an out of the way place.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: You had better go to western Canada and stop being so parochial.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
It lacks proximity to medical, psychiatric and university facilities. Difficulties will arise in helping the offender avail himself of these services. Staff may become stagnant because of a lack of access to the academic world, consultative services and other community resources. I might tell my friend, who is snickering over there, that one of the concerns of the international

February 25, 1968
Supp ly

J ustice
penology group that met in Stockholm this summer was to site prisons in places where there would be a variety of such services. I think, for instance, of the complex which has developed around Kingston, which has excellent psychiatric and psychological assistance, good medical facilities, excellent facilities in the way of the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society, and a school of law. Because of the psychological care which has been available to many of these institutions they have been vastly improved. I can tell you that every one of the 60 students at Queen's Theological College is undergoing constant supervision and training in the various institutions in Kingston which include the Kingston maximum security penitentiary, Joyceville, Collin's Bay, and the prison for women.
I say that with the professional and expert assistance that is available, there is as much hope for the penitentiaries here. I am not impressed by the emphasis on architecture and the building program which will cost Canadians something like $110 million. Personally I hold the view that we have far too many people in Canada in prison.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: There are a few people I would like to see in jail.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Perhaps if the committee will bear with me I could refer to extracts from document No. 19 of Sunday, January 23, 1966, under the directorship of Ross McLean of the C.B.C. This is called "A Sense of Captivity". One inmate said:
You don't have to think. Everything's done for you. You sit back and sink into the weeds, you might say, and become an automat.
I am concerned about the separation of many people whom I have known in penitentiaries which I have had occasion to visit, people who have had long separation from their wives and children.
Listen to this:
In 1960 or 1959 I had a visit from my wife. At that time the visit was over, we were leaving the visit, and she was going out to North Gate. This working crew was coming in, and one of the men stepped out of the line to grab the baby, and the copper that was walking the men he yelled at him.
I said it's all right. Anyways he took the baby and held it, held the child, the boy in his arms, and you'd have to see the expression on this man's face and how sad this was! And this guy bugged me for months after till I came over here, asking me, how was the kid? Could I have a picture of your child? And this man was no degenerate, it was a normal man. Just this craving to see a child or to be able to pick up a baby again.

I happen to know of two or three cases which fall into this category. I am concerned for instance even about the limitation on the correspondence of the inmate to his wife. Here another inmate is speaking of the homosexual problem:
I don't know, it is hard to explain. Some person needs somebody else, because if you do not have somebody you fall apart yourself.
What does Mr. McGibbon, the commentator, say:
A prison is all the things we deny those who have offended us .... is a hiding place for mistakes we've made . . . problems we couldn't solve . . . guilts we can't abide ... is an institution of last resort. When all the other institutions . . . the homes, the schools, the churches, courts and counsellors . . . have failed. A prison is a state of mind where tensions you never quite walk off remain to (haunt) your dreams.
I am concerned too about some of the statistics we find in Canada. It is clear that many of the people at the present time are going to return. In fact some people say this figure is as high as 80 per cent. Ninety per cent of those in penitentiary will one day be released. If this is so, surely the great burden is to examine ways, means, and techniques to improve what I think in many respects is an ineffectual and ineffective prison system.
May I go on with some of the comments which we heard on this recent program. Again this is Mr. McGibbon:
Our Canadian prisons today are the price we pay for thinking that if we forget the criminal, he will cease to exist. But he will not cease to exist until we admit that he does exist and until we make it possible for him to learn to exist as a man in our free communities.
Again Mr. McGibbon:
-in prison the need for human dignity is such a shrieking thing.
Personally I do not believe we are making proper use of our prisons. I would like to see more of the special institutions. I am pressed in this direction by the fact that I had occasion during the war, early in 1940, to be involved with a group of 125 men released from Dorchester penitentiary. For a while I could not believe how these people who came from such a place really could be much use to their country. I did not think they knew very much. But it took me just a few weeks to develop a little humility and realize these were persons, just as myself, and maybe in some respects better than myself. When I look back over that group of 125 men, it seems to me we need more of the work camp approach as a technique of correction.
February 25, 1966

[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am depressed by the fact that inmates in the Canadian penitentiaries are employed for very short periods of time, in many instances only two and a half or three hours a day. Often the work is demoralizing and unproductive. It was Agnes McPhail of the C.C.F. party who years ago complained about the lack of work for prisoners. If that sounds Dickensonian I invite hon. members to read her speeches to see how absolutely right she was. I see no lack of logic in the suggestion that we should develop techniques whereby prisoners are paid for work, to encourage them and to help them to maintain their dignity. Perhaps they should not be paid full wages, but at least a portion of a wage.
I should like to see methods developed in respect of parole allowing prisoners to work hard in their special skills or at hard labour in order to decrease their period of incarceration. I am convinced that this could be done.
A year or more ago I made a proposal to the effect that we could develop our waste lands in the north through the use of prisoners who are serving time. I think back to my experience with those 125 men who learned to soldier with the first division, and how magnificent they were. I am convinced that if we used the arctic and transport equipment developed by the army, we could put these people on islands in the Arctic to develop bases, docks, landing strips and other communication facilities. It is my belief that these men would pull themselves together under such conditions and become eligible for parole, and some of them might even wish to remain there.
Here in this lovely part of Ontario I have studied by cruiser the wonderful Rideau canal system, built many years ago by Colonel By and the Royal Engineers. It is being allowed to fall to pieces in certain spots. I am convinced that inmates could perform the masonry required to repair this canal system. Surely this would give people in penitentiaries some encouragement to rehabilitate themselves. This whole idea might sound fanciful and ridiculous, but I do not believe that it is.
Perhaps these ideas sound logical to me because of my regular participation in the deliberations of inmates, many of whom I find are not very different from the members of my own family and my friends. Some of them have had far less in the way of privileges, while some of them, I agree, are vicious, psychotic and dangerous requiring permanent custody. If we in Canada are deeply
Supply-Justice
concerned about civil rights and the rights of individuals we should start by studying what is happening in our prisons.
I have been impressed by the work that Isabel Macneill has done at Kingston.

Isabel Macneill, as so many of you will remember, came from the maritimes from a fine old Halifax family. Many will remember that she commanded the Wrens during the war. Nickels who stands high in the services being carried out at Kingston penitentiary.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I note that my hon. friend remembers him as the padre of his frigate some years ago. These two fine individuals have done a great deal for the penitentiaries they have served. Let me quote what Isabel Macneill has said:
Prison itself ... is the punishment and everything that happens after admission . . . should be geared to re-education-
She has suggested that 60 per cent of the girls now in prison have been convicted under narcotics charges. Let me present very briefly the impressions of one or two of these inmates. One states:
My first night here I couldn't even sleep because all I could see was the bars, you know the reflection of the bars on the wall and uh . . . it made me cry in fact I cried half the night.
I don't think it could be described really. It's just three walls and the bars, a floor and ceiling and a bed.
Another inmate states:
I'm in my 50's and there are other around in this age group, and I'm learning more about crime than I'll ever learn in my life. I don't know whether this is important for my rehabilitation.
I think it is about time we got some of those people out of those maximum security prisons into open prisons.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? I note that the

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
hon. member for the Northwest Territories is in his seat, which prompts me to ask the hon. member for Leeds whether he has consulted with that hon. member about his idea to send these convicts to the north, and whether the hon. member for the Northwest Territories is in agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I have discussed this idea with several hon. members. I have discussed it with other people who have been involved in the exploration and development of the north. I am not suggesting that many inmates should be sent to the north. Perhaps I should explain my proposal. It is my belief that men who are physically fit should be allowed to volunteer as members of crews to be moved up to the north by aircraft-travelling with light equipment, sleeping in tents, in an effort to further develop these waste areas.
The men who could stick out this kind of existence would be far better off than living in a small cell. I have discussed this with other individuals and I am sure there are a lot of young men in our institutions in excellent physical condition who would be delighted to be given an opportunity to work amid the glories of our northland. I have had the opportunity of visiting the north, particularly during my university days. I am sure this program would give these men a challenge and would help them change their whole attitude.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to say a good deal more about this subject, but I will not at this time as I am sure there are other members who wish to contribute to the debate. In concluding let me say that I do agree with what has been said by Alan Peyton, a prison superintendent. He said:
An offender must be punished, I don't argue about that; but to punish and not restore, that is the greatest of all offences.
We are spending far too much money today to keep each man serving time in a penitentiary. I suggest the maintenance cost runs between $2,700 and $3,000 per year. To that figure one must add an additional $2,000 paid in support of many prisoners' families. I suggest if we have that kind of money to spend we should spend it in ways which will encourage these people to rehabilitate themselves. As Walter Scott said, "It's no fish ye're buying, it's men's lives". There are many fellow Canadians who are still obscurely fighting the last fight of virtue, still clinging to some rag of honour, the poor jewel of their souls. They need our help.

I believe we have much to do and I am grateful that the Prime Minister has seen fit to reform and reconstruct the justice department in order that we should pay real attention to crime in all its aspects, including the rehabilitation of prisoners.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief this afternoon. I wish to refute the suggestions made by the hon. member for Leeds who recommends that dangerous convicts should be taken out of maximum security and set free in the north. I want to point out the folly in the hon. member's suggestion that we should use inmates in public works for the repair or construction of the Rideau canal and other projects in Canada. Public works should continue to be done on contract by the lowest bidder.
After listening to arguments about civil liberties and justice I want to point out a strange paradox that exists. The government is not inspiring confidence on the part of the public through their policies. According to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice this man Spencer is under continuous surveillance in spite of the fact there has been no trial or inquiry into his alleged actions. On the other hand, the inmates in our penal institutions who have been tried and convicted should be kept under surveillance and enforced security, yet this is not the case.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Therefore we may deduce that there are civil liberties and penal liberties, apparently. This situation should not exist in the sense that has recently been demonstrated. I refer to the recent prison break from Collin's Bay penitentiary. This break took place on Wednesday, February 9, when four dangerous men were successful in escaping from that institution. It has been said around Parliament Hill and the area from which I come that it is now easier to get out of a penitentiary than it is to get in.
My constituency is adjacent to Kingston and the institution there. The people in the area of Bay of Quinte, Kingston and the upper St. Lawrence are very concerned about these prison breaks and the security in our institutions. Security in our penal institutions should at all times be beyond criticism and must indeed be constant and rigidly enforced.
I would refer to the questions I placed on the order paper and point out that they have been there long enough for answers to be
February 25, 1966



given. I waited a reasonable length of time after the recapture of these men before asking these questions. The first question is to be found on page 82 of the order paper and was lodged with the government on February 15:
Has there been a special inquiry into the factors and/or persons contributing to the prison break of three dangerous prisoners from Collin's Bay penitentiary on Wednesday, February 9, 1966, who were later captured near St. Catharines and, if so, will the government report to the house the findings resulting from this inquiry?
Until I get answers to these questions I must assume that the attitude of the government to this matter is negative. I understand that the prison staff were forewarned of this break. If this is so there is absolutely no excuse for this lack of security and carelessness.
The fact that vigilance was at the time not practised or performed by the guards closest to the escapees set off a chain of events that is most regrettable and in fact can never be corrected. I understand that most of these prisoners were nearing the date when they would be eligible for parole. What a sad case this is. Their action has terminated the chance of their ever being paroled. They have ruined their lives by their actions and will now serve the original sentences plus an additional, appropriate term for breaking out of prison. Moreover, they have grievously jeopardized and harmed the life of their innocent female victim. I refer to the woman they captured, robbed, tortured and in fact are alleged to have criminally assaulted. All this damage was done because security, vigilance and the action we require from guards in these circumstances was absent or was not performed. I understand that the rifle of one of the guards would not fire. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I would quote my question that appears on page 93 of the order paper. This question was lodged with the government on February 18:
With respect to the recent escape of prisoners of the Collin's Bay penitentiary, was the utilization of one of the rifles issued to a guard impeded by grease on the bolt?
This question concerns the public of this country who deserve and expect protection. My next question was:
Do guards at penitentiaries have daily inspection of their rifles and. if not, what is the reason?
Then I asked:
Is it mandatory that penitentiary guards shoot in order to prevent an escape of a prisoner or prisoners and. if not, what is the reason?
We were informed that one guard did not, would not or refused to shoot at the escapees.
Supply-Justice
The question is, why? This is a very serious question, Mr. Chairman. We are dealing with the basic element, the real meaning of government, the protection of persons and property. I for one, and I believe all hon. members will not allow this principle to be weakened.
In summing up my point, Mr. Chairman, I would say it is evident to all hon. members that the level of security in this penal institution has been lowered or at least is of a variable nature. This has been demonstrated by the regrettable incident to which I have referred. I ask that this matter and all matters pertaining to penal security, the action of guards, the rules and the enforcement thereof in our penal institutions as they apply to vigilance and the full practice of strict enforcement of security, be referred to our standing committee on justice at the earliest possible date.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to preface my remarks by adding my congratulations to the Solicitor General upon his appointment to this portfolio and for his forward-looking approach with regard to penal problems and their solutions. I also extend my best wishes to the Minister of Justice in the difficult job he has ahead, and agree with the government that it was necessary to separate the numerous departments that were previously within the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice. I thought that any remarks I made this afternoon would be anti-climactic to those of the hon. member for Yukon, but I notice he is adopting a legal ploy and is trying to get as much information as he can from the government before making a frontal attack.
I direct my remarks to the ever-increasing problem of bankruptcy and state categorically that the Canadian public and in particular the Canadian businessman is amazed and shocked at the inaction of government with regard to amendments to the Bankruptcy Act which are necessary to deal with fraudulent company and personal bankruptcies. There has been no revision of the act since 1949, in spite of active interest by concerned groups in the business community. My hon. friend the member for Greenwood the other day set forth the many organizations which have presented briefs to Ministers of Justice and in regard to which no action has been taken. For example, a very full brief from the Board of Trade of Metropolitan Toronto was submitted in 1961 and in 1963 a full brief was

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
submitted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants. Then in 1965 we had the Mercier report which dealt with fraudulent bankruptcies in Quebec as they affected the Department of Revenue of that province.
In addition to these briefs there have been numerous articles in periodicals and newspapers concerning the probems of bankruptcy. I refer to an article under the dateline Friday, February 4, which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star, written by Alastair Dow who reports a speech by Mr. Biddell, the President of Clarkson, Gordon and Company, one of Canada's largest firms of bankruptcy trustees. This article reads:
Bankruptcies, he said, have grown from "a minor problem to a national disgrace" since the last time the Bankruptcy Act was revised, in 1949. He added that the tendency of government is to ignore the problem, to sweep it under the rug . . .
Biddell came from a modest family, and he says it agitates him to rub shoulders every day with people who have taken a financial beating because of bankruptcy abuses. He has seized upon his mission also because of the inaction of government.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
"If there's anything that motivates me, it's people who won't move to solve a problem".
The problem, as Biddell sees it, is far from insurmountable. "It wouldn't be difficult at all to revise the Bankruptcy Act.
"This isn't going to be a one-shot war. You have to change laws to fill the loopholes as people get smarter, the way the Income Tax Act is frequently revised. It's about time we got started on the Bankruptcy Act".
The day is long past when bankruptcies could be considered a private matter between debtors and creditors.
This indicates the attitude of the president of one of the largest firms of bankruptcy trustees in the country. Added to that is the growing number of bankruptcies that have taken place in the last two years. At page 27 of the brief submitted by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants in October 1963 the following statement appears:
From the point of view of government responsibility, bankruptcy is big business. The administration of the Superintendent's Department in 1961 included the supervision of the administration of some 3,876 estates with estimated liabilities in excess of $157,000,000.
That was in 1961. In 1963, according to the January issue of the Canadian Credit Institute publication:
The number of bankruptcies and resultant defaulted liabilities have been growing at an alarming rate and amounted to 3,677 commercial failures and $196 million in defaulted liabilities in 1963 compared with 1,303 and $25 million respectively in 1950.
According to Dun and Bradstreet, they have calculated that 2,597 businesses went

broke in 1965, leaving a trail of debts totaling $175,855,000. So you can appreciate the growing increase in the number of bankruptcies from 1950 to the present day.
One might ask, why this great increase in the number of bankruptcies? I think it is the duty of members to find the reasons for this, and I hope to offer constructive criticism. I think we have to look at the classes of persons involved, and their attitudes, to determine just what are the reasons for these bankruptcies.
The first class of person, Mr. Chairman, would include the previous minister, and perhaps the present minister, and their attitude toward the conduct of bankruptcy matters. I think the attitude that suggests that the provincial government is primarily responsible for enforcement of the administration of justice in connection with criminal activities under the Bankruptcy Act, and that they only are responsible for the supervision of trustees, is a wrong attitude to take. I suggest that the problem should be tackled on the same level as we tackle problems under the Combines Investigation Act.
I suggest that we should set up a separate department to investigate these allegedly fraudulent bankruptcies, a department staffed by men with experience in accountancy and company law. I also suggest we retain special counsel to prosecute the cases. This is done in the case of combines investigation, and although there could be many criticisms of it I think that the same practice should be followed.
I am sure that the Minister of Justice would agree he is having difficulty in the province of Ontario persuading the Attorney General of the province to set up a separate department to investigate these bankruptcies. I understand there is reluctance on the part of the Attorney General to appoint someone separate and apart to investigate these allegedly fraudulent bankruptcies. At the moment, my only knowledge of any investigations in Toronto are those conducted by two members of the fraud squad of Metropolitan Toronto who are not experienced enough in corporate law relating to fraudulent bankruptcies to be very familiar with the subject. The crown attorney in Toronto, because of shortage of staff, is very reluctant to let one of his assistant crown counsel devote his full time to processing these fraudulent bankruptcy cases. It is public knowledge that these cases take a minimum of four to eight weeks to process.
February 25, 1966

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware of the provisions of section 3(5) of the Bankruptcy Act, which sets forth that the superintendent of bankruptcy, federal office, may engage such accountants or other persons as he may deem advisable to conduct any action outside of the office of the superintendent?

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, I am familiar with that provision. I am also familiar with the fact that the Minister of Justice has not taken appropriate action under that provision. I am just dealing with what happened in Toronto, Ontario, in regard to the fraudulent bankruptcies that occurred in that area. So here you have an Attorney General reluctant to appoint somebody to conduct an investigation. You also have two men on the fraud squad who are inexperienced in these intricate matters; and you have the crown attorney for the city of Toronto unable to let one of his assistants devote his full time to the subj ect.
I would agree with the hon. member for Yukon that what is really needed is an investigation of these bankruptcies on a national scale by the R.C.M.P. You need officers from the R.C.M.P. as well as accountants and lawyers familiar with company law. You need that type of person, rather than having to depend on various branches of provincial administration. That would be my respectful submission, Mr. Chairman, to the minister in connection with this problem. The second reason for the difficulties in bankruptcy has been the improper actions of the trustees. In some areas it would appear that competition between bankruptcies and proposals has brought about practices which involve virtual collusion between debtors and the trustees they employ, which is against the interests of the creditors. To strengthen that point I should like to read briefly from the Mercier report, wherein is set forth the actions of some of the trustees in Quebec. I would suggest that the same comments could be applied to the actions of some of the trustees in Ontario.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This is on page 11 of the Mercier report:
In virtue of the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, the trustees represent the interests of the creditors and nearly all their powers are conditioned by the approval of the inspectors appointed
Supply-Justice
by the creditors. It was shown that, in practice, certain trustees are the "potentates" of the quasitotality of the bankruptcies which they administer. Because of their extensive knowledge in bankruptcy matters, they usually manoeuvre the unsuspecting inspectors as if they were puppets. In many instances, it was established that certain trustees had cleverly arranged the appointment of one or more of the inspectors. It is all so easy that the creditors and inspectors in good faith showed a disinterest that the Commission has already brought to light.
Amongst the many grievances lodged against the trustees during the inquiry, the Commission held the following: To begin with, there is the conflict of interest. On this point, it seems necessary to remember that in many instances of assignment or proposal, a conflict of interest is found between the trustee, who acts for the bankrupt and who is in fact his client, and the creditors whom he has the obligation to protect.
Then I continue:
In a number of cases, the trustee was paid his fees in advance from the bankrupt or obtained a bond: this situation presents itself particularly in summary matters where there are practically no assets. There is a real conflict since, for the trustee, it is no longer a question of protecting the creditors but of liberating a debtor.
The report goes on at page 12:
By incidence, it was noted that a number of trustees were more or less in the "business" of bankruptcy, and, in order to administer their offices with all the disbursements involved, they need a flow of bankruptcies. In order to effect this, many saw the advantage of maintaining good relations with the debtors rather than with the creditors.
On page 13 the report continues:
In many cases, it was noted that money, which was supposed to have been distributed to the creditors as dividends, was retained in the bank, without valid reason, for a considerable period after the settlement of certain bankruptcies.
Then the report takes a slash at some members of the legal profession. It says:
Testimonies, including one by a member of the bar, revealed that it is current practice, for certain trustees, to require and receive hush-money from lawyers representing the interests of secured creditors or of bidders promising in return not to oppose proceedings taken by the latter. It was also observed that certain representatives of trustees are using blackmail in order to obtain certain advantages or interest in the businesses which are operating under proposal.
These are some of the allegations which have been made against the conduct of trustees. I would ask the minister to strengthen the office of superintendent with regard to the issuance of licences and the conduct of these trustees.
The same comments could be applied to a third class, being the class of inspectors.

February 25, 1966
Supply-Justice
Again, the Mercier report sets forth the condemnation of the actions of inspectors, consisting in many cases almost of direct collusion or acquiescence in the actions of the trustees.
Another class which I think deserves criticism and reform is the class of finance companies. At page 16 of the Mercier report it says:
We should mention that the practice of several finance companies, to realize their security without accounting to anyone, does not seem to satisfy the elementary exigencies of equity towards the creditors, specially after taking cognizance of the facts discovered by the Commission during the inquiry, when it has been established that the agent or mandatory of a finance company, charged with realizing the security, was none other than an individual of doubtful reputation having been involved in rings of fraudulent bankruptcies.
In order that bankruptcy companies should be brought to the attention of the minister-

As the hon. member for Yukon has said, it may be only a partial list. However, I believe the institute has brought forward recommendations which are well worthy of consideration. One of them is that there should be an amendment of the act with regard to the definition of a related person. They recommend that we incorporate into the act the provisions set out in section 139 subsections (5) and (6) of the Income Tax Act to stop this practice of placing all the assets in one company and all the liabilities in another.
The second suggestion relating to persons who are not dealing at arm's length is that any conveyances to persons who are not dealing at arm's length with the debtor should be considered fraudulent if they are made within a period of 12 months rather than within a period of three months as set forth under the present act. The third recommendation relates to persons who are not dealing at arm's length being unable to vote with regard to a proposal set forth by the debtor, unless it is to vote against the acceptance of that proposal. These are all matters of which we should take immediate cognizance. Legislation should be brought down forthwith to amend the act accordingly.
The second area to be considered is the area of proposals which a debtor makes. In this field there have been many abuses. Those most frequently complained of by creditors are that many debtors lodge proposals with the trustee without the means or even the intention of carrying them out. It is alleged that in many instances the purpose of such frivolous proposals is merely to enable the debtor to use the stay of proceedings obtained thereby in order to dispose of his assets to the detriment of his creditors.
Many debtors are assisted in such a scheme by the absence of any direct responsibility on the trustee acting in the proposal to control the debtors' assets. Again, the brief sets forth methods whereby actions of this type could be controlled.
The third recommendation relates to the re-organization of the superintendent's office.
Supply-Justice
Some of the recommendations set forth are as follows: 1. The appointment of an assistant deputy minister to the superintendent of bankruptcy. It is high time such an appointment was made. 2. The appointment of three assistants to the superintendent of bankruptcy whose duties would be to supervise the activities of registrars, official receivers and trustees; investigations of bankruptcy frauds and the processing of trustees' statements. I am sure the hon. member for Yukon would agree that in the past one of the problems has been that the burden of investigations has usually fallen upon the shoulders of the creditors rather than their being any active participation by the minister and his staff. This has been a most serious problem. Here again I agree with the hon. member that it will take a national force to combat the situation facing us today.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Again I would refer him to subsection 5 of section 3. The expense of paying accountants and other persons to engage in these investigations is payable from the appropriation of the office of the superintendent of bankruptcy. If the minister had been exercising the authority granted to him the cost would have been paid in this way and there would have been no need for it to fall on the shoulders of the creditors. That is, if the minister is doing his job.

maintopic: EIGHT OF MEMBER FOR MONTMAGNY-L'ISLET TO VOTE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is again underlining the need for immediate action by the minister to advise the superintendent to look into these matters regardless of the expense, because he has the authority to do so under the act. I agree most heartily with that.
A final area in which this problem has arisen is that of personal bankruptcies. There has to be a new approach to the question of personal bankruptcy-a new attitude toward persons whose income is derived from salaries or wages, who have incurred large debts by overspending and who then find the present procedures an easy way in which to avoid the repayment of their debts. We must discover a method of ensuring an orderly payment of a bankrupt's debts, under budgetary control and supervision, in order that the debtor may repay his creditors 100 per cent. What I am saying is this: We need to take stronger action with regard to company bankruptcies, but we must also take a hard look at the activities of individuals who are taking advantage of the present provisions of

February 25. 1966
Supply-Justice
the act in order to avoid the repayment of their debts. I believe the Canadian public and Canadian businessmen in particular demand immediate action for the protection of all Canadians to restore confidence in the business world and to give strength to the enforcement of the law.

In the ten minutes or so remaining, it will be quite impossible to deal with the variety of subjects which warrant consideration. I have sat here throughout the debate waiting for the Minister of Justice, or one of the other ministers who now share the throne of justice, to rise and explain themselves with regard to the matters which have been referred to with such clarity again this afternoon, not only by members of the official opposition but by the hon. member for York-Humber who spoke as a Liberal supporting the government. His speech, I should have thought, would have been answered.
I wish to refer to the Spencer case. I was not here when this subject was discussed in the house the day before yesterday. But I say at once that the decision not to hold a judicial investigation into this matter is a gross perversion of the elementary principles of freedom. The excuse which is given, namely that the security of this nation would be interfered with, is simply a smokescreen, and nothing else.
This man has been pilloried before the Canadian people. He has been given no opportunity to answer. His name was spread across the nation by the minister, in a totally unjustified way, and it is now stated after all this cloak and dagger drama that he is not complaining. Well, that adds to questions that arise. Why? Across this nation people are beginning to wonder whether there is something behind this case that has not been revealed.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I do not have the time now to refer in detail to the press release of May 8, issued by the Department of External Affairs, but I shall do so on an appropriate occasion. It should be read and reread. It either meant something, or this particular case happened to arise at a time when something had to be brought up in order to cover up the revelations that were being made in the Rivard case.
From time to time it happens that security is undermined, but never before has a man been identified with a government failing to act. Why? Is there any reason to believe that

if Spencer speaks his threat will be implemented to the effect that heads will roll, or heads will swim? If there is not, then why not an investigation by judges, in secret if you will, allowing them to make their report? Otherwise I can only say that the Bill of Rights has been entirely denied-every principle of it.
What is the government covering up? Nothing, the minister says. If it has nothing to cover up why not have a judicial inquiry into this matter? That is the same kind of answer as the hon. gentleman's predecessor gave on November 23, 1964 when the hon. member for Yukon was speaking, and the former minister of justice said, "It is lies," and then within an hour admitted that he knew previously, and it was true.

I want to be perfectly clear. Now we are again getting the same kind of answer in connection with Spencer. This afternoon the hon. member for York-Humber spoke the language of wisdom when he asked for action in this regard, but the government sits quiet. Why? Whose are the heads? Where are the heads that are going to fall or to swim? Spencer does not object. I would like to have the opportunity of examining Spencer and finding out what happened here, because it is a strange thing that he does not object. But he says if anybody dares do anything something is going to happen. I will come back to that next week. I thought this afternoon we would be able to get through, that the minister would get up and answer, but I can tell him and those associated with him that until this is answered we have a responsibility.
I now wish to deal with another matter in the few minutes remaining at my disposal. I have overwhelming respect for the R.C.M.P. I have said that before, and down through the years. I have known them since the days of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. But we have had the Rivard case, we have had the views expressed by the chief justice. If there is one thing above everything else that must be maintained it is that not even by way of suggestion may the mounted police, shall the mounted police, or dare the mounted police be used for anything that savours of the likelihood of politics, and they are being put in an impossible position by this government.
The commissioner of the mounted police ought not to be rushing into print. He ought not be the one who rises in defence of his force. That is the job of the minister. The commissioner ought not to be writing letters to the papers, and I am thinking of the letter that he wrote on November 25. No commissioner, however distinguished his record, in the past ever followed the course of writing
Supply-Justice
the letter which the present one wrote because of an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of July 8, and which stated:
The short, easy-going lawyer from Sorel, Quebec, moved smoothly and swiftly yesterday into the political hotseat of the Pearson administration, the justice portfolio.
Without waiting for the official swearing-in ceremony, Canada's new justice minister, Lucien Cardin, set up a meeting with R.C.M.P. Commissioner George B. McClellan.
It went on to say:
Commissioner McClellan and the force have been subjected to Increasingly heavy public and private criticism in recent months, especially since the publication of the Dorion report which censured the R.C.M.P.'s handling of the investigation of charges of attempted bribery and influence-peddling in the Lucien Rivard affair.
The two men met privately in Mr. Cardin's old office shortly after the former public works minister was sworn into his new job by Governor General George Vanier at Government House.
Mr. Cardin described the meeting as informal. "I don't like formal meetings," he explained.
That was in July, and on November 25 a letter appeared from the commissioner. I am not admonishing for what was done. I am pointing out that this kind of thing will grow if a government does not scrupulously assure that the R.C.M.P. shall not be in any way held to come under the scrutiny of those who have political purposes in mind. The commissioner wrote this letter:
I have listened with interest recently to your radio advertising campaign stressing the accuracy of Globe and Mail news coverage.
In this atmosphere, you may wish to have a few words with the writer of the attached article (regarding an informal conference between Mr. McClellan and Lucien Cardin) which appeared in the Globe and Mail and which is completely false. No such meeting took place between the Minister of Justice and myself as described by your reporter.
And this is signed "George B. McClellan, Commissioner, R.C.M.P., Ottawa."
It ends up with an editorial note at the bottom saying:
The source of the information in the article referred to was Mr. Lucien Cardin, the Minister of Justice.
I am simply pointing out that the mounted police must be preserved meticulously and courageously from the kind of thing that has been creeping in during the last couple of years, and it is on that I want to speak when the opportunity comes again.

the second reading of Bill C-ll, to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act (Hog and Egg prices stabilized half-yearly and regionally).
He said: Mr. Speaker, my bill is not a bill in respect of which heads will roll, but instead where eggs are rolling. I think the bill as outlined is one by which, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Agricultural Stabilization Act to:
(1)	provide deficiency payments for eggs, hogs, etc., on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted average price;
(2)	have these deficiency payments made semi-annually instead of annually as at the present time.
In the explanatory notes it is explained that the purpose of this bill is to provide that the Agricultural Stabilization Board shall establish the base prices for hogs and eggs at and for every half-year instead of every year. A second purpose is to provide that these prices shall be determined regionally instead of Canada-wide and applied within the appropriate region: that is, the Atlantic provinces, the central provinces, the prairie provinces and British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to introduce this resolution for debate. This is not the first time I have placed this resolution on the order paper. It had been debated before without result or action taken by the government, although it is of great importance to the egg producers and hog producers of Canada, particularly to the prairie provinces.
You will notice in the motion, Mr. Speaker, that it provides deficiency payments for eggs and hogs on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted average price.
[Mr. Cardin.l
I suggest that these deficiency payments be made semi-annually instead of annually at the present time. This is very important to the egg producers in the three prairie provinces, because when the weighted average price in Canada is calculated, the producers never receive a deficiency payment that is anywhere in line with the over-all price plus the deficiency payments received in other areas of the country.
To justify my argument I should like to give hon. members an example of the year 1964-65. The statement was made that the price support for eggs will be continued another year at the present level, the federal agricultural department has announced. In the year ending next September 30, the Agricultural Stabilization Board will support the price of grade A large eggs by a deficiency payment program at a national weighted average of 34 cents a dozen to producers.
The statement goes on to say that in the 1963-64 period, the national average price amounted to 32 cents a dozen, resulting in a deficiency payment of .02 cents a dozen to producers. The maximum for a deficiency payment, according to the Agricultural Stabilization Board remains unchanged-4,000 per producer.
This covers grade A extra large, grade A large, and grade A medium sizes. The program this year, however, provides that payments shall not be made on quantities of eggs that would result in payments of less than $2.00 per individual. To be eligible for payment producers must be registered with the stabilization board and must have marketed their eggs either through registered grading stations or to retail outlets as producer-graders.
In 1965 during the month of May on the prairies the price received for grade A large eggs averaged 17 cents to 19 cents per dozen, but at the same time in the east the average price received by the producers during this period was 35 cents. In Victoria and Vancouver it was 31 cents to 32 cents, and in Toronto and other cities it was as high as 35 cents.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Also for the record I should like to give you an example of another year. In 1962 when the average price in Canada was 33 cents per dozen, at the end of the year the stabilization board calculated that the deficiency payments for that year would be one cent per dozen. One cent per dozen for grade
February 25, 1966

A large was received right across the country, but in Saskatchewan the average price for the year was only 28J cents per dozen. If the price had been calculated on a regional basis, the producers on the prairies-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-would have received 52 cents per dozen deficiency payment bringing the price up to 34 cents, which was the board price. Instead of that they received only one cent per dozen because the average national price was 33 cents.
This in my opinion was unjust as far as the producers in the three prairie provinces are concerned. It is my opinion that deficiency payments should be calculated on a regional basis, and I would establish the regions in this way: B.C. one area, the three prairie provinces another area, eastern Canada a third area and the maritime provinces a fourth area. Deficiency payments should be calculated on a semi-annual basis because there are times of the year when the production is very high and the prices are low. There are other seasons of the year when prices are high and production is low.
This same suggestion should be applied to deficiency payments on hogs. As far as hogs are concerned, this matter may be more important than it is in respect of eggs. Everyone knows that in the fall when the farmers bring their hogs to the market prices are usually down. The farmers who are able to market their hogs in the spring always get a little better price. If deficiency payments were made on a semi-annual basis it would mean that whatever deficiency payments were paid to the farmers who received low prices for their hogs in the fall would be cancelled out by the higher prices received in the spring.
This is a very important issue to the farmer. Promises were made by all parties during the election campaign that this matter would be looked into. Proposals have been advocated by farm organizations across the country and I think it is time that the government paid attention to this situation and amended the stabilization act.
At the present time the stabilization board makes these payments from October 1 to September 30. That is the year for the calculation of these deficiency payments and that is the year in which prices are averaged.
I am aware of the stand taken by the stabilization board. This is not the first time I have presented this case to the minister. In a memorandum issued by the stabilization 23033-116J

board on regional price supports they argued that if deficiency payments were calculated on the basis of the difference between regional prices and regional support levels such a procedure would not provide over the years any significant benefit to the producer. They stated that, in general, regional support levels based on a ten year average for the regions would vary between regions during the support year. Thus payments would be essentially the same as those that might be made under a national program.
In addition the stabilization board suggested that such a policy would present many administrative difficulties, as it would doubtlessly lead to a proliferation of regions since our normal geographic and provincial boundaries do not, of necessity, coincide with marketing areas. It is my opinion that that is the biggest reason why the stabilization board is opposed to this idea. The problems associated with the selling in one region of commodities produced in another would make such a program almost unworkable, according to the board.
I cannot agree with this viewpoint. I think the administrative difficulties could be overcome and that the board's assumption that, under normal conditions, where prices are lowest costs are lowest, is not valid. The production cost to the egg producers on the prairies is the same as in other areas where prices are high. I do not think there is very much difference between the price of feed in the east and in the west. The cost of bringing the product to market areas is not very much higher in the east than it is on the prairies.
There are many other factors involved in producing hogs and eggs that are similar, but the prices for these products are much higher in the east than they are in the west. We in the west with our low prices are helping the producers of eggs and hogs in the east to qualify for higher deficiency payments.
I have brought this problem to the attention of the house on more than one occasion. Political parties when electioneering have told people that this problem needs to be solved, but when parliament assembles and the Throne Speech is read there is never any mention of proposed measures to alleviate this situation.
I note that the member on the other side of the house who intends to reply to my remarks is the same member who replied on other occasions. Perhaps that hon. member and I should get together to look at this

problem from a reasonable point of view. I am sure he could be convinced that this bill deserves approval and that my proposals should be implemented at this time.

speechtext:
to areas where production is scaled to demand. This of course distorts prices received in such regions. Egg production is characteristically seasonal in output. Although some provinces like British Columbia reveal only slight variations, others such as Saskatchewan reveal marked variations in marketings of eggs from one part of the year to the other. As a result of the variations in supply, prices react accordingly, with low prices generally prevailing in the December to May period and high prices from August to November.
Previous proponents of seasonal deficiency payments have suggested that the actual prices received during low price quarters be compared with the national prescribed price and the resultant deficiency be provided in the form of a payment to all producers. Since the actual market price is generally lower in the seasonally flush period of the year than the prescribed price, and higher than the prescribed price in the lower period of production, payments would generally be always made for the former period and not the latter.
This would have the undesirable effect of encouraging production and marketing during the flush period, in order to receive a payment, which would aggravate the seasonal swings in output creating greater seasonal discrepancies in marketings and in prices. Seasonal variations in marketings and the accompanying swings in prices tend to reduce consumption through consumer resistance to high prices and a concurrent switch to substitute products.
During the past several years the egg industry has come a long way in overcoming the seasonal patterns inherent in the industry. To change a seasonal deficiency payment scheme now would destroy years of painstaking evolution to a more even pattern of marketing. Price stability in the market for eggs and hogs is important. It is best achieved by allowing these products to flow freely to consumers in a nationally based market. In this manner the movement of commodities from surplus to deficit areas is made easier and prices tend to seek levels consistent with supplies in the immediate area, taking into account the cost of transportation to or from the market in question depending upon its position as a surplus or deficit area.
If artificial barriers are set up in Canada through the introduction of four separate
Private Bills
regions of support, as suggested in the proposed amendment to the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the free flow of eggs and hogs will be restrained as producers seek to obtain the advantages of regional support and price fluctuations will become more marked from region to region as price levels tend to be dependent on regional supply conditions only. Thus price stability will suffer.
In addition, as I have indicated before, not only will there be greater disparity in prices from region to region but also the introduction of semi-annual deficiency payments will' encourage the marketing of eggs and hogs in the low-priced six-month period when payments are most likely, aggravating seasonal price fluctuations from which the whole industry will suffer. Fair returns for labour investment cannot be maintained if prices are not stabilized.
Regional and semi-annual payments to egg producers may benefit initially the many small producers in western Canada but in the long run, as price differentials widen from region to region and seasonal swings increase, the small producer may not survive. In fact, while a Saskatchewan producer may become eligible for a larger payment than his Ontario counterpart, only a small proportion of the producers in this province will market sufficient eggs to claim the maximum benefit, while in Ontario the reverse is true. For example, in 1964 only 6.7 per cent of the 1,697 claimants in Saskatchewan claimed the maximum $80 payments while 27.6 per cent of the 12,383 Ontario claimants did so. It appears then, that only the large producers in the west will benefit from a regional scheme of payment.
As far as hogs are concerned, the calculation of regional and semi-annual prescribed prices in 1964 using the 1964 national percentage of the base price, that is 88.3 per cent, would provide no benefit to producers. In all parts of Canada the regional weighted average price remained above the regionally calculated prescribed price. Thus there is no benefit to be derived from such a scheme even in the short run.
It goes without saying that a plan involving the calculation of several separate base prices, several separate prescribed prices and the administration of several separate regions and seasons for payment will add tremendously to the government's cost of operation. If the benefits accruing from such a complicated method of stabilization outweigh the social costs involved in its administration,

February 25, 1966

then the added burden to the taxpaying public may be justified; otherwise it is not justified.
In conclusion, if we implemented the proposal to change the present deficiency payment scheme for hogs and eggs to one on a regional and semi-annual basis it could, instead of being beneficial to the agricultural producers concerned, disrupt marketing patterns, cause greater price instability, discriminate among producers because of location, create consumer dissatisfaction in the product, undoubtedly affecting consumption, benefit the large scale producer in certain regions and discriminate unduly against small producers in other regions. In effect, there is nothing to be gained by either industry in changing to the regional and seasonal system of support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak just briefly in support of the bill which has again this session been introduced by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp). There may be validity in some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Asselin), but even if these prices had been calculated regionally there would have been times when the deficiency payment would not in fact have been any higher than it was in some other specific year. We do not deny that. But the fact is that there were cases-and I think the hon. member who introduced this bill outlined them very well-when the total price in so far as producers in Saskatchewan were concerned did not come up to the national average because they received so much less in the marketplace during the course of the year.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Under the old price support policy for hogs a few years ago, I recall this was a continual source of irritation to hog producers in Alberta. For the most part, hogs produced in Alberta were consumed either in Alberta or shipped to the Vancouver area on the west coast. While this price support policy was in effect the support price was established by taking into account the base price in Toronto and then subtracting the cost of freight from Calgary or Edmonton. That was not satisfactory at all, and as far as we were concerned there was no justification for it.
As I said, almost all the hogs produced in Alberta-I presume the same is true for Saskatchewan-were consumed in the area. In other words, there was no direct relationship

between the price paid in Toronto and the price paid in western markets because there was very little movement of that meat from the west to the Toronto market.
I also want to comment briefly on the question whether or not it would be beneficial to have a half-yearly calculation made, rather than an annual calculation as at the present time. I do not know how important this will be over a long period of time when one considers the ten-year average under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, but I believe there should be some detailed analysis made of the differences that may occur in the deficiency payments which have been made.
I noted when the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) introduced his bill that he made some calculations, and the figures he produced indicated that at least in two or three instances there would have been an improvement in the deficiency payment made if it had been calculated on a half-yearly basis. Therefore, until the argument advanced by the hon. member in introducing this bill has been explained away or destroyed, in the interests of the producers of eggs and hogs in certain areas I think we have to accept this study of prices and that there has been some disadvantage to these producers because the figures were calculated on an annual basis rather than a semi-annual basis.
One of the interesting point made by the hon. member who introduced the bill is this. According to some of the figures he used, when some of the producers in Saskatchewan added up the total market price received for their eggs, plus the deficiency payment which they received later, they were still several cents per dozen below the national average of 34 cents per dozen. When a similar bill to this was introduced in 1957 and 1958, I think it was intended that there should be a floor price established for these products and that producers all across the country would be brought up to that floor price, which would be determined by a ten-year average. Yet in the practical application of the present system it simply does not turn out that way.
I just wanted to say, Mr. Speaker, that I support the hon. member's bill, at least in his attempt to correct some of the discrepancies he has described. As I said before, for the most part I believe that the eggs and hogs produced in the regions outlined by the hon. member in introducing the bill are consumed in those same areas. If that is the case there is surely no reason to penalize certain areas
