by taking into account prices in other areas when deficiency payments are established.
So, Mr. Speaker, I simply say that we should either accept this bill and amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act in accordance with the provisions of the bill, or else we should have a far more satisfactory and complete explanation from those in the government who are responsible for the administration of this act, indicating that no real injustice is being done to producers in certain areas of the country.

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to congratulate my hon. friend, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), for bringing this matter before the house once more for thorough discussion. I might even go along with him as far as the semi-annual payment is concerned.
He said in his opening remarks that this provision would be more beneficial to the prairie provinces. This is Canada, Mr. Speaker. We cannot look at the problem from a regional angle alone. Therefore I must take exception to this proposal of my hon. friend from a national point of view, and from a national point of view only.
I think we should start at the beginning. What we must decide is whether the changes my hon. friend has requested should be made; and, if they should, whether it is actually possible to make the changes. Let us consider these matters in turn.
First of all, we must examine the proposition that producers everywhere should receive the same unit of return from one coast to the other. The very suggestion that the return should be uniform implies that there is something radically wrong with a pricing system which results in produce being sold at different prices in different parts of the country. In this regard it seems desirable to note some of the regional price variations, and in particular to explain just why they exist.
Let us start in western Canada with Canadian western wheat, which moves eastward to the market. The price the farmer receives at the country elevator declines as the distance between him and Fort William increases. Farmers living in western Saskatchewan certainly receive considerably less than those in Manitoba. In each case the cost of transportation is deducted from the basic Fort William price to determine each farmer's return.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The same situation exists in Ontario and in Quebec with respect to potatoes grown in the Maritimes. Potatoes are grown in Ontario and in Quebec, and what has to be taken into consideration when considering potatoes from the Maritimes is transportation.
The same situation applies to fluid milk going to Toronto from producers in Ontario. Those producers that are closer to the main market receive more, because of lower transportation costs. The same general principle operates wherever products are sold competitively and production takes place at varying distances from a common market. This explains why prices quoted for cattle, hogs or eggs on western Canadian markets must always be somewhat lower than those quoted at Montreal and Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, it also explains why farmers are willing to sell eggs right at home, right at the farm, for much less than they would accept if they took those articles to market. At the same time it does not necessarily follow that the difference between prices paid in varying places is simply the difference in cost of transportation. However, we know that that is not so. It has a great deal to do with whether there is a surplus, or a limited amount of the product to be sold at the time. All these things have to be taken into consideration. In fact unit prices and costs vary from region to region.

May I continue with what I was about to say. Under a competitive situation such as we have in Canadian agriculture, farmers in western Canada could not keep selling livestock products at lower prices than obtained by Ontario or Quebec farmers, unless costs to western farmers were lower than those to farmers in central Canada by at least enough to cover the cost of moving their products eastward.
After all, Mr. Speaker, the real test of whether farmers in one region make as much profit as those in another is found in the extent of their willingness to continue producing. Under competitive conditions farm products do tend to be produced where they can be produced most efficiently. I think we all realize that.
If this government, or any government as far as that is concerned, agreed to pay transportation costs by varying the size of deficiency payments from region to region, in the manner suggested, I think that farmers would tend to produce more where costs, other than transportation costs, were low, in order to get a unit return equal to that of producers producing in higher cost regions.
In time, of course, actions of farmers producing in low cost production areas would tend to reduce the level of the nationally weighted average market price, and therefore would reduce the level of the support price which is closely related to that market price. In the meantime, however, the farm production pattern of the country would be seriously disrupted and the costs to the government would be tremendously increased.
In the few remarks that I have made I feel that I have shown that it would be undesirable to pay these costs. For one thing, the act of giving different sized payments to farmers in different regions would certainly cause dissension among those farmers. For example, if the government gave a large deficiency payment to producers in one region, and gave a very small payment or no payment to producers in another region, I suggest that farmers in the latter region would object strenuously. They would claim that the government, by providing farmers in the former regions with large payments, was providing them with a special subsidy and that this payment or subsidy would improve the competitive position of farmers in the former region as compared with themselves. In other words, farmers in the latter region, receiving 
no payment or very little payment, would feel that there has been gross discrimination against them.
In other words, those farmers would feel that there had been gross discrimination against them, enabling farmers in regions where they received subsidies to enrich themselves through unfair competition.
May I just add this: Boy, oh, boy, I should not like to be in the shoes of the member of parliament representing a region where small payments or no payments to producers were made. If this were so, and if I were depending on the farm vote, perhaps there would be one less member on this side of the house.
The next important factor to consider is that a regional type of program would tend to remove a producer's incentive to dispose of his products to the best possible advantage. Let me illustrate this: There is little doubt that if a farmer, say in Saskatchewan, knew that he was sure to get a deficiency payment equal to the difference between the market price for producer in his own region and the national support price, he would not very likely try hard to move his eggs or hogs or produce to a higher priced market. The cost of the support program to taxpayers would be increased to the extent that producers failed to get the highest possible market price for their produce.
It is well to note that this tendency for farmers to lose their marketing incentive exists wherever deficiency programs are administered on any kind of regional basis. I am going to give one little example. If farmers in Saskatchewan had a regionally guaranteed support price of 27 cents a dozen for eggs, they would not feel any great incentive to seek somewhat higher prices in other regions if they found the market price in Saskatchewan falling below the 27 cents level.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In connection with that type of regional program which farmers and their organizations have recommended, and which I think my hon. friend has also recommended, tending to give farmers everywhere the same total unit return, it would not make any difference where farming was carried on. It is necessary to recognize that all those who advocate this kind of program must assume that market prices in various regions will always be lower than the national support price. Any such assumption however is entirely invalid. The fact is that the regional market prices will
February 25, 1966

actually be higher than the national support price whenever the supply in the various regions is limited in proportion to the demand-in other words, in short supply.
Assuming the number and location of the regions to have been agreed upon, the next problem would be to administer the program in such a way as to insure that all produce was actually sold in the same region in which it was produced. Let me point out that the cost of getting farm products to a considerably higher-priced market in an adjoining region may be no greater, or even less, than the cost of getting it to a lower-priced but equally distant market in their own region. Under a regionally administered program, however, it would presumably be considered quite unfair for any farmers to receive a larger deficiency payment because market prices in their own particular region were lower than in a neighbouring region in which they had actually done their selling.
At the same time it is obvious that any attempt to force all farmers to do their marketing within their own regional boundaries would not only involve a lot of expensive policing but would seriously interfere with market practices and marketing connections which have long been specially advantageous to the particular farmers concerned. Note that word "force". We are hearing a lot of that word these days, and I do not agree with it all, I can tell hon. members that much.
To get back to the policing question: I do not know about the feelings of any of the members across the way, or even on this side of the house, but we seem to have reached a state where an extra police force has to be set up to look after everything parliament does, whether it is in the field of income tax, pensions, or anything else. I can tell hon. members that the independent farmer is going down fighting. He will fight any suggestions that he should be forced to do something he does not want to do. From this angle alone I think we are dealing with a ticklish problem.
It would be exceedingly unpopular, partly because it would be interfering with the farmer's freedom. And, my God, these days it is only the farm people of Canada who appear to have a little freedom left. It would be unpopular because, as I said, it would interfere with the farmer's freedom to decide where to market and also because it would force him to shift from a higher priced to a lower priced market outlet. At the same time 23033-117

it would be uneconomic since it would prevent a considerable amount of produce from following normal marketing channels.
To sum up I should like to say this. From what has just been said it should be obvious that adoption of a regionally-based type of program would lead to some extremely difficult and unpopular if not absolutely impossible administrative situations. It should be equally clear that it would result in very serious confusion and misunderstanding in producer ranks generally.
If farmers find difficulty in understanding how a single standard yearly deficiency payment is calculated it would really be hard work explaining to them the variation in deficiency payments from region to region. I think that on a national basis the proposal is completely out of fine.

In the two minutes that are left this evening on the subject of this bill I should like to strike a blow for the city man. In my constituency we have one farm and that is the farm belonging to the university of British Columbia. Its area is gradually dwindling and it will soon be wiped out by the engineering department and other departments of that university. Then we shall be entirely a city constituency.

Can hon. members recall a year or so ago when there was a disastrous earthquake in Peru? This country, like all good countries, went to the help of the Peruvians by shipping them aid. They needed bandages, iodine, medical supplies and things of that kind. What did we send them, sir? We sent them a shipload of luncheon meat. Why? We did it because it embarrasses us to have so much luncheon meat on hand. The price of hogs, the price of eggs and the price of butter are kept up at artificial levels until we have storehouses filled with these commodities. So when there is a disaster we use it as an opportunity to ship out of the country whatever stores are embarrassing us at the moment. That is why we shipped carloads of luncheon meat to the poor Peruvians who were looking for bandages.
